<<removeobjective "day_2">> I woke up feeling wrong. Not pain-wrong. That was the strange part. I lay still for a moment, staring at the ceiling. The water stain shaped like a horse was still there. The cracks in the plaster were still there. Morning light filtered through the shutters in thin golden lines, painting the wall in stripes the color of watered honey. Normal. Familiar. By now, the shadow should be thick and dark, heading toward a proper beard. Instead, it was... patchy. Light in places. As if some of the follicles had decided to take the morning off. Green eyes. Present. Deep-set, hooded lids, the same intense stare that had been looking back at me from reflective surfaces since I was old enough to care about reflective surfaces. The scar through my left eyebrow. Present. Some people pray. I do math. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That's the most Mira thing you've ever said. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I know. I'm a brand. <</dialog>> She opened her eyes. Looked at me. The amber gaze warm in the stairwell's lamplight, gold-edged, the eyes that had been watching me sleep and carrying me through the dark and mapping goblin mines from memory while I bled. <<dialog "Mira">> Three days. We have three days to get your leg working, prepare for the escort, and avoid Grent until the arrangement is official. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> About Grent <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> He'll find us. He always does. But now when he does, we have Voss's arrangement as a shield. He can't override the accounts department. Nobody overrides the person who knows where the money is. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You said that before. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Because it's the truest thing I know about how power works. Swords are impressive. Muscles are useful. But the person with the ledger runs the world, and everyone else is just providing content for the entries. <</dialog>> We emerged from the warehouse into the Dockside air salt, tar, fish guts, the perpetual olfactory punishment of a district that existed to move cargo and didn't care about the comfort of the people doing the moving. The morning was gray and damp. The dock workers were already at it, hauling and shouting and living their lives in the spaces between the crates. My leg hurt. The walk to Dockside had cost me the ankle was swelling again inside the boot, the calf wound sending sharp reminders with every stride that healing wasn't the same as healed. But the debt had a structure now. A plan. A woman with ink-stained fingers and a ledger had written something down, and whatever she'd written had the weight of institutional authority behind it. We walked back to the Broken Antler. Slowly. My pace dictating, Mira matching it without complaint, without comment, without the passive-aggressive velocity she deployed when she thought I was being slow for emotional rather than medical reasons. This time the slowness was legitimate and she respected it the way she respected all legitimate limitations with patience and the quiet understanding that the body would deliver what the body could deliver, and pushing harder would cost more than waiting. We were halfway through the Market District when Mira said it. <<dialog "Mira">> Voss is interesting. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Interesting how? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Interesting in the way that people who control information are always interesting. She knew where we were staying. She knew Grent would find us. She had the escort contract ready not because we asked for it, but because she'd already identified us as potential assets and was waiting for us to walk in so she could deploy us. We didn't negotiate. We were handled. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You sound impressed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm impressed by anyone who's better at strategy than I am. It happens rarely, so I notice when it does. Voss is playing a game that's three moves ahead of where we're standing. I want to know what game. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The Consortium's game. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Maybe. Or maybe her own. People like Voss people who sit in rooms full of numbers and see the patterns underneath they always have their own game. The institution is just the board they play it on. <</dialog>> She let the thought settle. We kept walking. The Broken Antler appeared at the end of the street squat, familiar, smelling of pipe smoke and the accumulated misery of a building that had been hosting other people's bad days since before either of us was born. <<set $day_3_3 = false>> <<link "Go to the Broken Antler">> <<regionmap "valdmere">> <</link>><<set $day_3_3 = true>> We went inside. Ordered ale. Sat in our booth and waited for Grent. Finally he came. He filled the doorframe the way a cork fills a bottle. Oilskin cloak dripping, scar-tissue face arranged in the expression of a man who'd come to collect and wasn't in the mood for conversation. His small eyes found us in the corner booth with the targeting speed of someone who'd been looking for exactly two broke mercenaries and had found them precisely where broke mercenaries tended to sit. He crossed the common room in four strides that shook the floorboards and sat down across from us without invitation. Again. The same deliberate placement of his bulk. The same territorial claiming of space. <<dialog "Grent">> You hit the mine. <</dialog>> Not a question. Grent's information network was apparently as efficient as the rest of him. <<dialog "Aldric">> We hit the mine. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> You came out empty-handed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> We came out alive. Which, given that the warband was closer to twenty than fifteen, I consider a professional achievement. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> The Consortium considers recovered cargo a professional achievement. Breathing is a baseline expectation, not a bonus. I want my advance back. Twenty silver. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We don't have twenty silver. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Then we have a problem. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We have a solution. We spoke with Voss at the Dockside warehouse today morning. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> You spoke with Voss. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I spoke with Voss. She's agreed to waive the advance repayment contingent on our completion of a secondary contract. Escort job surveyor to a ruins site east of here. Three days, round trip. Fifteen silver each on completion, plus the debt cleared. The Consortium gets its money's worth. You get your contract fulfilled. We get to eat next week. Everyone wins. <</dialog>> Grent looked at her. Then at me. His eyes traveled down to my leg the bandaged calf, the swollen ankle visible above my boot line, the general state of someone who'd been through a meat grinder and come out the cheap end. <<dialog "Grent">> You look like hell. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You should see the goblins. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> I'm not interested in the goblins. I'm interested in whether a sellsword who can barely stand is going to be able to escort a Consortium surveyor through bandit territory without getting himself or the surveyor killed. Because if the answer is no, then this arrangement wastes everyone's time and I still want my twenty silver. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> He'll be ready. The leg is healing fast. Give us three days and he'll be mobile. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Three days. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Three days. We depart on the fourth morning with the surveyor, complete the escort, deliver Voss's cargo assessment, and square the books. You get your money's worth of mercenary labor. We get clear of the debt. Clean and simple. <</dialog>> Grent's jaw moved the grinding motion of a man chewing on a decision. He looked at my leg one more time. Looked at my face. Something shifted behind those small, calculating eyes the mental arithmetic of a man who dealt in risk and reward, balancing the cost of chasing twenty silver from two broke sellswords against the potential return of getting free labor. <<dialog "Grent">> Voss will be in touch with the escort details. Don't make me come back here. <</dialog>> He stood. The chair scraped against the floor. He pulled his oilskin hood up and left without another word, the door banging shut behind him with a finality that rattled the windows. The orange cat, disturbed by the bang, leaped off the bar and stalked away with the offended dignity of a creature that had been deeply inconvenienced. <<dialog "Mira">> That went well. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> He looked like he wanted to break my other leg. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> He looked like he wanted to break both your legs AND your arms. But he didn't, which means Voss's arrangement holds. Crisis managed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> For now. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> For now is all we've ever had. I'm going to the Consortium warehouse to confirm the escort details. You stay here. Rest the leg. Every hour of healing matters. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What am I supposed to do sitting in a room all day? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Not die. Not reopen your stitches. Not make any financial commitments. The bar is low. I believe in you. <</dialog>> She squeezed my shoulder the same brief, compressed gesture of affection that was her substitute for everything a normal person might express with words and left. The tavern door closed behind her with significantly less violence than Grent's departure, which was Mira's version of being gentle. <<addobjective "day_3" "Rest and recover">> [[Alone in the room...|day_3_4]]The room was quiet in a way it hadn't been since we arrived in Valdmere. Mira was gone out negotiating our survival at the Consortium warehouse, doing the work she was better at than me, which was most work that didn't involve swinging a sword. I was alone with the lumpy bed, the horse-shaped water stain, and the growing suspicion that something was happening to my body that I couldn't explain. I sat on the edge of the bed. Unwrapped the calf bandage. The wound was I stared at it. Blinked. Stared again. The twelve sutures Ysolde had placed with such meticulous care were sitting in skin that looked like it had been healing for a week. The angry redness was gone. The swelling had reduced by half. The edges of the wound were closed, the skin around them pink and healthy, the kind of healthy that suggested new growth rather than inflammation. The stitches themselves were almost ready to come out the tissue had knit together underneath them with a speed that made no medical sense. This was three or four days of healing compressed into less than twenty-four hours. I touched the area around the wound. Gentle pressure. No heat. No tenderness. No sign of the infection that had been setting in when Ysolde extracted those eight splinters from my muscle last night. Whatever her compound was doing, it was doing it with the focused efficiency of an entire temple of healers working in shifts. I rewrapped the bandage and sat by the window. The market district was busy below a normal day in Valdmere. Carts rattling over cobblestones. Merchants adjusting their stall displays. A group of children chasing a spotted dog through the crowd, their laughter high and sharp and uncomplicated by the kind of problems that adults accumulated like barnacles on a hull. Normal life. The kind of life that cost money and required stability and assumed a body that stayed the same from one day to the next. My hands were resting on the windowsill. I looked at them. Big hands. A swordsman's hands. Wide palms, thick fingers, calluses layered over calluses the hard ridges of keratin that ten years of gripping steel had built up like geological strata. Scars across the knuckles from fights I'd won and fights I'd lost and a few that had ended in draws where both participants walked away bloody and claimed victory to different audiences. The calluses were thinner. I pressed my thumb against the rough wood of the windowsill and the texture hit me like a shout. Every grain, every splinter, every imperfection in the wood vivid and specific, as if someone had polished the nerve endings in my fingertips to a higher resolution. I could feel details I'd never noticed before. The subtle ridges of the wood grain. The difference in temperature between the sunlit spots and the shaded ones. The faint vibration of a cart rolling past on the street below, transmitted through the building's structure and into the windowsill and into my skin. I flexed my hands. Opened. Closed. They looked the same. Almost. The calluses were there but their edges were softer, as if they'd been sanded down overnight. The rough skin of my palms was smoother to the touch still a working man's hands, still scarred and thick-fingered, but with a new layer of sensitivity underneath the toughness, like wearing thin gloves you could feel through. I dropped my hands. Shook them out. After-effects. The compound was a powerful healing agent and it was working on everything not just the wound, but the surrounding tissue, the skin, the nerves. Heightened sensitivity was a side effect. A temporary one. It would fade as the compound worked its way through my system. [[Time passes...|day_3_5]]I spent an hour sitting by that window, flexing my hands and trying not to think. I failed at the not-thinking part. The brain is a poor servant when you tell it not to examine something the instruction itself becomes an obsession, the forbidden thought growing larger and more detailed the harder you push it away. Don't think about your skin. Now all I could feel was my skin. Don't think about your calluses. Now my palms were the center of my universe. I stood up. Walked across the room. Walked back. The ankle protested a dull ache, manageable, improving by the hour. The calf wound was a distant memory of pain, the stitches pulling slightly with each step but nothing more. My belt felt different. I stopped. Looked down. Tugged at the leather. It was at the same notch the one I'd been using since Thornwall, the comfortable middle position that accommodated a full stomach and an empty one. But it was marginally looser. Not enough to slip. Not enough that I'd notice in normal circumstances. But I was not in normal circumstances and I was noticing everything, and the belt was sitting a fraction lower on my hips than it had yesterday. Weight loss. I'd bled. I'd barely eaten. Blood loss and reduced appetite equaled weight fluctuation. Normal. Explainable. I rubbed my jaw. The stubble was there rough under my fingers, the scratch of three days' growth. But one spot along my upper jaw, just below the sideburn, was smooth. Not smooth like a missed spot shaving. Smooth like nothing was growing there. I pressed, feeling for the follicles, the tiny bumps that indicated hair would return. Nothing. Just skin, soft and even. I pulled up my tunic and looked at my chest. The pectorals were the same thick, hard, the flat planes of muscle that came from years of sword work. The dark hair was there, concentrated in the center with a trail running down my midline toward my navel. But was it thinner? I tried to remember what my chest hair looked like yesterday, the day before, last week. You don't catalog your own chest hair. You don't pay attention to the specific density of growth on your pectorals unless someone gives you a reason to. No one had given me a reason. Yet. I dropped the tunic. Turned to the mirror. Leaned close. My face. The same face. Square jaw, green eyes, scar through the eyebrow. The same face I'd worn for twenty-six years, the face that looked back at me from every polished shield and every still pond and every lover's eyes. Was it softer? I pressed my fingers against my cheekbone. Against my jaw. Against the ridge of my brow. The bones were the same. The structure was identical. But the skin over them smoother. The weathered, sun-roughened texture that had been my face's defining characteristic for years was... diminished. Not gone. Just less. Like the difference between old parchment and new parchment same material, different miles. <<dialog "Aldric">> It's the healing compound. It's a side effect. It'll pass. <</dialog>> I said it to the mirror. The mirror didn't argue, which I took as agreement even though mirrors aren't qualified to practice medicine. <<set $day_3_6_a = false>> [[Go downstairs...|broken_antler]] [[Stay inside room|day_3_4_b]]<<set $day_3_6_a = true>> Boredom drove me downstairs. Boredom and a thirst that bad ale could technically satisfy, and the need to be somewhere other than a small room with a small mirror and a growing collection of questions I didn't want to ask. The common room was drowsy. Afternoon light slanting through the grimy windows, dust motes drifting in the beams like tiny lost travelers. A few day-drinkers at the bar. The innkeeper sweeping in his usual perfunctory manner the broom moving, technically, but the dirt's strategic position remaining unchanged. Lenna was at the bar. Not working afternoon off, casual clothes. The linen blouse buttoned to the collar, hair pulled back in the practical knot. No bodice, no presentation. The daylight version of her, which was simpler and younger and somehow more herself than the candlelit version had been. She was eating bread with honey and drinking tea, and she spotted my limp before she spotted my face. <<dialog "Lenna">> Gods, Aldric. What happened to your leg? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Goblin mine. Floor collapsed. I went through it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> The job from the other night? The one you wouldn't tell me about? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That's the one. It went about as well as you'd expect a job I wouldn't talk about to go. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> You should be resting. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm bad at resting. Resting requires sitting still and thinking, and right now my thoughts are not company I'd choose voluntarily. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> Then sit with me. I'm better company than your thoughts, and the tea is free if you flirt with the innkeeper's wife. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The innkeeper has a wife? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> The innkeeper has a wife, two children, and a collection of ceramic birds that he keeps in the back room. He's a deeply complicated man under all that indifference. Sit down. <</dialog>> I sat. She flagged the barmaid and ordered me an ale her money, not mine. A reversal of their previous transaction that made something warm shift in my chest. <<dialog "Aldric">> You don't have to <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> You bought an hour. I can buy an ale. Fair trade. Drink it. <</dialog>> The ale was the same terrible swill the Antler always served, but it tasted better coming from someone else's coin. We sat together at the bar, her tea steaming, my ale flat, the afternoon light making the common room almost pleasant if you squinted past the grime. She told me about herself. Not the professional version the real one. Father was a fisherman who worked the Valdmere harbor until his back gave out. Mother died when Lenna was twelve the coughing sickness, the one that took the poor and the crowded first. She'd started at the Antler at seventeen because the innkeeper's wife took pity on her and the work was steady and the customers were rarely worse than rude. <<dialog "Lenna">> I'm saving. Every extra copper goes into a box under my bed. When I have enough, I'm opening a seamstress shop. I'm good with a needle my mother taught me before she got sick. I can do repairs, alterations, basic tailoring. Nothing fancy but solid work. The kind of work that feeds you without requiring you to take your clothes off. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> How close are you? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> Another year. Maybe two. The rent on a shop in the lower market is seven silver a month, and I need a three-month deposit plus materials. It adds up. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You'll get there. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> I will. Stubbornness runs in my family. My father fished the harbor for thirty years even after his back went bad. He'd go out in the morning hunched over like a question mark and come back at night with enough fish to feed us. Stubbornness is the poor person's talent. It doesn't cost anything and it works when everything else fails. <</dialog>> I told her about Dunmore. The farm. The lord who took the land not through battle or conquest, but through paperwork and taxes and the slow, grinding bureaucracy of power applied to people too small to fight it. My father drinking himself into a grave after the fields that had been in his family for three generations were signed away by a clerk who'd never set foot on them. My mother moving in with her sister. My brother apprenticing to a blacksmith. Me, taking up the sword because it was the one trade that didn't require land or a guild membership or a willingness to pretend the world was fair. <<dialog "Lenna">> We're the same, you and me. Different trade, same story. People who lost the ground under their feet and had to build something new from nothing. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You're building something. I'm just swinging a sword and hoping the money lasts until the next job. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Lenna">> That's building too. Different materials, same project. Survival is construction, Aldric. Every day you're alive, you've built another floor on the building. <</dialog>> She squeezed my hand when she left. Her fingers were warm, the callus on her thumb pressing against my knuckle and the sensation was sharper than it should have been, the skin-to-skin contact registering with a vividness that made me blink. <<dialog "Lenna">> Rest, Aldric. Whatever that woman gave you for the leg, let it work. <</dialog>> She walked away. I watched her go. The freckles on the back of her neck, visible where the hair was pulled up. Copper constellations on warm skin. I wanted to count them, which was a stupid thing to want, and yet. I finished my ale. Went back upstairs. Sat by the window. Flexed my hands on the windowsill and felt every grain of the wood with a clarity that was becoming harder to explain. [[Mira returns...|day_3_7]]Mira was gone. The room was mine, and the silence was the kind that invites investigation. I sat on the bed. Looked at my hands again. The calluses were definitely thinner I wasn't imagining it. The hard ridges I'd built over a decade of swordwork were softening at the edges, the skin underneath smoother and more tender than I'd ever felt it. When I gripped the edge of the bed frame, the wood felt different in my palm more detailed, more present, as if my hand was learning a new language of texture. I stood and walked to the mirror. Checked my jaw again. The smooth spot below the sideburn was still there a patch of bare skin where stubble should have been. I searched for others. Found one on my chin, slightly to the left of center. The hair around it was thinner than the rest, the three-day growth barely a shadow. I pulled my tunic up. Looked at my chest. The pectorals were unchanged thick, hard, the flat slabs of muscle that I'd been carrying since my teens. But the hair over them was thinner. I could see more skin through it than yesterday. Individual hairs seemed finer, lighter, as if they were in retreat not gone, but diminishing, like a forest thinning at the edges. I touched my right nipple. Not deliberately my hand grazed it while pulling the tunic down, an accidental contact that shouldn't have registered. It registered. A jolt of sensation shot from the nipple straight through my chest and into my stomach and down into my groin, a hot wire of feeling that made me inhale sharply through my teeth. Not pain. Not pleasure, exactly. Something in between a sensitivity so intense that the lightest touch was overwhelming, the nerve endings screaming at a volume they'd never used before. <<dialog "Aldric">> What the fuck. <</dialog>> I said it to the empty room. The room didn't answer. I touched the other nipple. Deliberately this time. Just a fingertip, the lightest possible pressure. The same jolt. Electric. Immediate. A sensation that traveled from the nipple through internal pathways I didn't know I had, connecting to places in my body that had never been connected to my chest before. My stomach clenched. My groin tightened. My breathing went shallow. That had never happened. Not from a casual touch. Not from pressure that light. My nipples had always been just... there. Functional parts of anatomy that served no particular purpose and generated no particular sensation. Now they were live wires, hypersensitive to the point of being distracting. I dropped my tunic. Pressed my palms flat against my thighs and breathed slowly until the sensation faded. It took longer than it should have. The echoes of it lingered in my chest like the ring of a struck bell, slowly diminishing but refusing to go entirely silent. The compound. Ysolde's vial. Whatever was healing my leg at superhuman speed was also doing something to my nervous system rewiring connections, amplifying responses, changing the way my body processed sensation. It was healing me and altering me at the same time, and I was sitting in a rented room in a bad tavern watching it happen in real time and unable to do anything about it except catalog the changes and tell myself they were temporary. They had to be temporary. I sat by the window. Watched the street. Waited for Mira. Tried very hard not to touch my chest. <<addobjective "day_3" "Wait for Mira to return">> [[Mira returns...|day_3_7]]The afternoon shadows were lengthening across the market district when I heard her boots on the stairs. The particular rhythm of Mira's walk quick, precise, two steps at a time was as familiar as my own heartbeat. I knew before the door opened whether she was carrying good news or bad by the speed of her approach. Tonight she was moving at "mixed news" pace neither the brisk efficiency of a problem solved nor the measured deliberation of a disaster in progress. The door opened. She came in carrying a canvas bag of supplies and the expression of a woman who had negotiated hard, won most of what she wanted, and was tired enough to acknowledge it. <<dialog "Mira">> Good news and complicated news. Which do you want first? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Good news. I've had enough complicated for one day. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The escort job is confirmed. Voss signed the contract fifteen silver each on completion, advance debt wiped clean. We depart in three days with the surveyor. His name is Hadden Marsh. He's a fussy little man with spectacles and ink-stained fingers who looks like he's never been outdoors voluntarily. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The complicated news? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The route. <</dialog>> She set the supply bag on the bed and pulled out a map a real one, purchased from a cartographer's stall, marked with roads and settlements and the kind of topographical detail that turned "somewhere east" into a landscape of specific choices and specific dangers. She unfolded it on the bed. Her finger traced a line from Valdmere eastward. <<dialog "Mira">> The surveyor's ruins site is two days east on the Ashenmoor Road. We escort him there, wait while he does his catalogs, escort him back. Three days total. Straightforward. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That doesn't sound complicated. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The Ashenmoor Road. Aldric. The same road we took to the Greymire mine. The same road where the Consortium's caravan was hit. The same road that a goblin warband of twenty-odd has been raiding for weeks. <</dialog>> She tapped the map. The escarpment where the mine sat was marked a small notation in the cartographer's precise hand, labeled "Greymire (abandoned)." It was four leagues east of Valdmere. The surveyor's ruins site was marked further along the same road another six leagues beyond the mine. The route passed directly through the warband's known operating range. <<dialog "Mira">> We killed maybe eight in the mine. Maybe ten. That leaves a dozen, give or take, who are angry and territorial and who just watched two sellswords carve through their home and walk out alive. Goblins remember faces, Aldric and they remember the ones attached to bodies that killed their kin. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> We'll be on the road, not in the mine. They hit caravans ambush and retreat. Two armed escorts with a single light-travel surveyor aren't the same target as a loaded cargo wagon. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Maybe. Or maybe a warband that just lost a third of its fighters is desperate enough to hit anything that moves through their territory, regardless of how armed it looks. Desperation makes goblins creative and creative goblins are the dangerous kind. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You're saying it's too risky. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm saying it's the only job we have, the route goes through hostile territory, and you'll be walking it on a leg that was impaled two days ago. I'm not saying it's too risky. I'm saying the risk needs to be managed, and managing it starts with knowing exactly what we're walking into. <</dialog>> She was right. She was always right about risk the professional assessment of a woman whose survival depended on accurate threat calculation. The route was the route. The goblins were the goblins. The leg was the leg. None of these variables were negotiable. What was negotiable was how we prepared for the intersection of all three. <<dialog "Mira">> There's more. The surveyor Marsh. Voss told me about him. He has conditions. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Conditions. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Consortium assessors aren't soldiers. They're academics with expense accounts and a deeply inflated sense of their own importance. Marsh has requirements: no travel after dark, hot food at camp, his equipment carried separately from our gear, and this is the one that made me want to hit Voss he insists on a daily written progress report filed at each waypoint. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> A daily written progress report. On an escort job. Through goblin territory. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> "The Consortium requires documentation of all contracted activities," Voss said. With a straight face. While signing a contract that's sending two half-broke mercenaries and a man who's afraid of dirt into a forest full of things that eat people. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Can you write the reports? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'll write the reports. My handwriting is better than yours anyway. You write like a drunk spider fell in an inkwell and tried to escape across parchment. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That's harsh. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It's accurate. I've seen your signature. The "A" looks like a tent that collapsed and the rest looks like a seismograph during an earthquake. <</dialog>> She folded the map. Set it aside. Began unpacking the supply bag fresh bandages, a pot of wound salve from a market herbalist, bread, dried meat, two apples. Small, slightly bruised, but real fruit, the first we'd had in days. She laid everything out on the bed with the organized precision of a woman who'd packed for survival a hundred times and treated it like an art form. <<dialog "Aldric">> Three days until we leave. I need to be mobile by then. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> How's the leg? <</dialog>> I stood. Walked across the room. Walked back. The ankle was sore but stable the kind of ache you could ignore on a march if you wrapped it right and didn't think about it too hard. The calf wound was a memory, the stitches sitting in tissue that had healed around them with impossible speed. <<dialog "Mira">> You're walking. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm walking. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You were barely standing this morning. That healer's compound is <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Working. Yes. Very fast. Unnaturally fast. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Anything else? Any other... effects? <</dialog>> She asked it carefully. Not casually Mira didn't do casual when she was interrogating. The question was precise, measured, and aimed at something she'd already noticed and was waiting for me to confirm. <<dialog "Aldric">> My hands feel different. Calluses are softer and my skin everything feels more sensitive. Like someone turned up the volume on every nerve in my body. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Is that all? <</dialog>> I hesitated. The nipple thing. The smooth patch on my jaw. The slightly looser belt. The barely-thinner chest hair. I could tell her all of it, lay it out like evidence on a table, and watch her face do the thing it did when she processed information that worried her the slight narrowing of the eyes, the almost imperceptible tightening of the jaw. <<dialog "Aldric">> My stubble's thinner in some spots and the belt feels a fraction loose. But I barely ate yesterday, so that's probably <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Weight loss. Blood loss. The healing compound using your body's resources. I tried to nap. Laid on the bed, closed my eyes, and instructed my mind to shut down for two hours. My mind responded by playing a detailed visualization of every possible way the mine job could go wrong, presented in vivid color with accompanying sound effects. Floor collapses. The sky was the color of old bruises deep purple, streaked with gray, the clouds still thick but emptied of rain. The air was cool and wet and smelled like everything the rain had touched and released: stone, earth, rotting leaves, the distant salt of the harbor. We left the Broken Antler armed and armored. Keeping my longsword sheathed to free both hands for balance. The ground was treacherous mud over rock, a recipe for broken ankles and bruised pride. The creek Grent had mentioned was running hard, swollen with two days of downpour, the water churning over stones with a sound like grinding teeth. The forest pressed in from both sides, dripping, dark, the trees rising like pillars in a cathedral built by something that hated visitors. We smelled the mine before we saw it. <<link "Go to the Mine">> <<worldmap>> <</link>><img src="img/scene/day_2/12.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> If you've never been downwind of a goblin camp, consider yourself blessed by whatever gods you pray to. It's not one bad smell. It's a symphony of bad smells, each one competing for dominance like drunks fighting for the last stool at the bar. Rotting meat. Unwashed bodies not the honest road-sweat stink of humans, but the sharp, acrid reek of creatures who'd never encountered the concept of bathing and would eat the soap if given the chance. Urine. Feces and over all of it, the sour chemical tang of the fungal paste goblins smoked in their pipes, which smelled like burning hair soaked in vinegar. It hit us from thirty paces. Mira wrinkled her nose which for her, with enhanced half-elf senses, must have been like getting slapped across the face with a dead fish wrapped in a dirty diaper. Fist up. Stop. I stopped. She pointed ahead and to the right. Through the scrub, I made out the mine entrance a ragged hole in the escarpment, framed by rotting timbers that sagged inward like the ribs of a dead animal. Eight feet wide, six feet tall. What had once been a proper entrance structure had collapsed into rubble, leaving a wound in the hillside. A goblin sat on a flat rock outside. Wrapped in a human-sized cloak stolen, probably from one of the dead caravan guards that pooled around it like a collapsed tent. A crude spear leaned against the rock beside it. Head down. Chin on chest. Asleep. The most pathetic sentry in the history of organized defense. I drew a finger across my throat. Kill it? Mira shook her head. Practical reasoning if it squeaked before dying, the sound would funnel into the mine like a megaphone. She held up one finger, pointed past the entrance. Go around. We crept wide. Generous berth, careful steps over loose rock. My heart was loud in my chest not fear exactly, but the heightened state that preceded every job, the animal awareness that sharpened everything. The crunch of gravel under my boots. The drip of water from the escarpment. The goblin's wheezing snores. We slipped past. Ducked into the mine. <<updateobjective "day_2" "Enter the mine and find the chemical storage shaft">> [[Go into the Mine|day_2_11]]<img src="img/scene/day_2/13.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> <<set $mcLocation = "upper_tunnels">> The air inside was different. Warmer. Heavier. It pressed against my face like a damp cloth, thick with wet stone and old iron and the goblin stench amplified by enclosure. The tunnel was wider than expected room for two abreast, ceiling high enough that I only ducked for the sagging support beams. Walls of rough-hewn stone, dark iron ore veins glinting dully in the faint orange glow from deeper in. Firelight. The camp. Mira nocked an arrow. The whisper of bowstring drawing back, the click of nock against string. She moved forward, arrow ready. I drew my longsword. In the tunnel it felt longer than usual, the blade nearly touching walls on either side at guard position. I'd have to fight tight. Short arcs. Jabs. Point work. Economy of motion in a space that left no room for anything else. We moved. The mine branched at forty paces. Main shaft ahead firelight, sleeping goblins, a chorus of guttural snoring that sounded like a barnyard having nightmares. Side tunnel left narrower, darker, cooler air carrying that sharp chemical smell. Goblin markings scratched into the stone at the junction. I couldn't read goblin script but one symbol was clear enough: a rectangle with lines radiating outward. A box. Storage. I pointed. Mira nodded. We took the side tunnel. [[Go to the Storage Shaft|day_2_12]]<img src="img/scene/day_2/14.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> <<set $mcLocation = "storage_shaft">> The deeper shaft was a different animal. Floor sloping steeply down, slick with moisture and fungal film each step felt like walking on wet sponges. Walls narrowing until my shoulders nearly brushed stone on both sides. Mira's bow scraped the ceiling and she hissed a curse the first sound either of us had made in ten minutes, echoing off the close walls like a shout. Freeze. Listen. Nothing. Snoring continued above. Undisturbed. We kept moving. The crates were twenty paces further down. Stacked against the tunnel wall behind a curtain of old mining canvas heavy waxed fabric draped over them like a tablecloth. The Consortium seal stamped into the wood: scales over ship's wheel. I counted by touch. Eight crates. Fingertips finding nail-heads on sealed lids. Four sealed. Two open but contents intact glass vials nestled in straw packing, cool and smooth. Two gutted, straw scattered, vials smashed. The chemical smell was strongest here, leaking from broken containers. <<dialog "Aldric">> Six recoverable. Four sealed, two open with contents. <</dialog>> I whispered so quietly the words barely had shape. Just breath with consonants. <<dialog "Mira">> Two each per trip. Three trips minimum. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Two. I'll rig carry harnesses from the canvas. <</dialog>> I reached for the mining canvas. Mira's hand clamped on my forearm. Iron-hard. Her fingers digging into the muscle with strength that always surprised me. In the near-dark, her eyes caught the faintest light and reflected it back two pale amber discs, wide and alert. Her head tilted, listening with ears that could hear a mouse fart at sixty paces. Then I heard it too. Footsteps. Purposeful. Coordinated. Multiple feet in formation, coming from the main shaft above. A horn blew. The sound was indescribable a high, wailing blast that filled the tunnels like water filling a bottle, bouncing off every surface, doubling and tripling. Crude instrument, carved animal horn, but in the enclosed space it was deafening. My ears rang. My teeth vibrated. The stone walls hummed with it. The sentry. Awake. A scent on the wind, a footprint in the mud, some goblin sixth sense. It knew. The horn died. In the silence: voices. Goblin common fast, harsh, consonants crashing into each other. Tone is universal. This tone said: Intruders. Find them. Kill them. <<dialog "Mira">> They know. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> They might not know where <</dialog>> Second horn blast. Closer. Much closer. From the junction above us. They knew exactly where. <<dialog "Aldric">> Move. <</dialog>> <<updateobjective "day_2" "Fight or flee?">> [[Fight or Flight|day_2_13]]I've made a lot of bad decisions in my life. The ale at the Broken Antler. The caravan job in Thornwall. The dwarf arm-wrestling incident in Kestwick. But I'd learned one thing from all of them: when the choice is between going deeper into the dark and fighting toward the light, you fight toward the light. <<dialog "Aldric">> Back through the main shaft. We punch out. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> There's going to be a lot of them between us and the exit. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Then we go through them. <</dialog>> <img src="img/scene/day_2/15.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Mira slung her bow and drew the short sword. She held it the way she always did like it owed her money and she was about to collect. We ran. The slope was treacherous going up the same fungal slime that made it unpleasant descending now turned it into a scramble, boots sliding on wet stone. My free hand bracing against the wall, sword hand keeping the blade forward. Mira behind me, breathing controlled and steady, the professional calm of someone who intended to survive this. We hit the junction at a run. Turned hard into the main shaft. Straight into five goblins. They were ugly. Knee-high, yellowish-green skin stretched tight over knobby bones, teeth jutting from their jaws at angles suggesting their dentist had been a rock slide. Small cunning eyes gleaming with the particular malice of creatures who survived by being mean and fast. Crude iron cleavers. Wooden shields reinforced with scavenged metal. No time to think. Body before brain training, instinct, ten years of muscle memory compressed into one explosive motion. My longsword came up in a tight arc that caught the first across the face. Wet crack. It dropped like a puppet with cut strings. The second went low classic goblin tactic, hamstring the tall-folk, let gravity and blood loss do the rest. It ducked under my blade and lunged for my knees. I stomped its weapon arm, felt the bones snap under my boot heel, and drove the sword through its back before it could scream. Behind me, Mira's bow sang she'd switched at the last moment, the confined range be damned. At ten paces in a tunnel, her arrows didn't arc. They punched. The third goblin took one through the eye socket and rocketed backward into the fourth, both going down in a shrieking tangle. The fifth turned to run. Its alarm screech rusty hinge being tortured bounced off every surface, echoing and re-echoing. So much for quiet. I stepped over the bodies. Blood goblin blood, thin and almost black, smelling like old copper and sour milk spattered my armor, my arms, my face. I wiped it from my eyes and pressed forward. The main shaft ahead. Firelight casting jumping shadows and there the quality of the light changing from orange to blue-gray where moonlight filtered in. The entrance. Forty paces. Fifty. Close enough to taste. More goblins poured from side tunnels. Six from the left, stumbling over each other. Three from an alcove I'd missed. Two dropped from a natural shelf above me a ledge I'd walked under without looking up, because I was an idiot and goblins were not. <img src="img/scene/day_2/16.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> The tunnel became a meat grinder. I fought the way I'd been taught control the center line, make them come to me. In a tunnel this narrow, they approached two abreast at most, which meant my longsword's reach was an advantage. I choked up on the grip, shortened my swings, used the blade like an oversized dagger. Jabs. Short slashes. Pommel strikes when they got too close. A goblin tried to climb over its dead companion and I caught it with a rising cut that opened its belly. It fell screaming, tangling the ones behind it. Mira was at my back. The short sword the weapon she hated doing the ugly close work she was terrifyingly good at. I could hear her behind me: the grunt of effort, the meaty impact of steel on flesh, creative obscenities directed at her weapon. An arrow whizzed past my ear she'd switched between bow and sword in a heartbeat, loosing a shot over my shoulder that took a goblin in the throat, then drawing the blade again for the next one. Thirty paces from the entrance. Twenty-five. Twenty. The floor gave out. <<updateobjective "day_2" "Fall into the pit">> <<changestat "health" -15>> <<changestat "energy" -15>> [[The Fall|day_2_14]]<img src="img/scene/day_2/17.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> <<set $mcLocation = "collapse_point">> Not all of it. A section maybe six feet across, where the old mining timbers underneath had finally surrendered to decades of moisture and rot. My right foot went first. One moment solid ground, the next the stone crumbled under my boot and my leg punched through into empty space. One thought oh no and then my left foot followed and I was falling. Three feet. Maybe four. Short fall but I landed wrong right leg twisting under me, ankle jamming between two shattered support beams like a log in a vise. The pain was instantaneous. White. Blinding. The kind that doesn't build but arrives fully formed, screaming. My longsword clattered from my grip. Splashed into water a foot of it, stagnant and foul, some old drainage channel. Cold, stinking, soaking through my clothes while my leg burned above it. I tried to move. Ankle locked between beams, wood pressing from both sides. Any shift sent a bolt of agony from my calf to my knee that blanked my vision at the edges and there I looked down, had to a splintered piece of timber driven deep into my right calf. A jagged wooden spike buried in the muscle. Blood flowing freely, turning the stagnant water dark. <<dialog "Mira">> Aldric! <</dialog>> Her face above me, framed by the ragged edges of the collapsed floor. <<dialog "Aldric">> My leg's pinned. Ankle's caught between the beams. <</dialog>> She dropped in. Landing in a crouch that barely splashed. Eyes going to my leg. Her jaw tightened one flicker of something that might have been fear before she locked it behind the professional mask. <<dialog "Mira">> The splinter <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I know. I can feel it. <</dialog>> Above us: the rapid patter of bare goblin feet on stone. Excited chittering. The sound predators make when they realize prey is trapped. Mira grabbed the beam pinning my ankle and pulled. It shifted an inch. The splinter in my calf moved with it not coming out, twisting, digging deeper. I bit the inside of my cheek so hard I tasted blood. <<dialog "Aldric">> Stop. You're making it worse. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I need to <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I know. Just give me a second. <</dialog>> I didn't get a second. The first goblin appeared at the pit's edge, peering down with gleaming eyes. It grinned goblins always grinned, it was the teeth and raised its cleaver. Mira's short sword took its head off. Single stroke, clean, the blade passing through the neck with barely a sound. The body stood there for a moment headless, still grinning then toppled into the pit between us, splashing rank water across my chest. <<dialog "Mira">> I need both hands. This is going to hurt. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> It already hurts. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It's going to hurt more. <</dialog>> <img src="img/scene/day_2/18.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> She sheathed the sword. Braced her feet against the pit wall. Grabbed the timber with both hands. She didn't pull this time she pushed, using her legs as leverage, her arms rigid, her whole body a lever. The beam groaned. Creaked. Shifted sideways with a scraping sound I felt in my teeth. The gap widened. Half an inch. An inch. Enough. I wrenched my foot free. The scream wasn't voluntary. It tore from my throat like something alive, and I buried it in my own forearm, biting down on leather and skin while my ankle throbbed with a deep grinding agony that pulsed in time with my heart. The splinter came out with the motion mostly. I could feel a piece still in there, broken off inside the muscle, my calf swelling around it. My ankle was a ruin. Expanding inside my boot, the leather tightening like a closing fist. Not broken I thought but torn. Twisted. Something ankles weren't meant to do. Two more goblins dropped in. Mira killed the first with a knife pulled from somewhere, the woman had weapons in every fold a quick practiced stab through the soft tissue of the throat. Wet gargling. Collapse. She kicked the second into the far wall hard enough that its skull cracked against stone like a dropped melon. I grabbed my longsword from the filthy water. Drove it through the stunned goblin's chest. The blade went in easy goblin ribs were thin and it spasmed once and went still. <<dialog "Mira">> Can you walk? <</dialog>> I tried weight on my right foot. The ankle folded. Not like a joint bending like a building collapsing. <<dialog "Aldric">> No. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Can you crawl? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Probably. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Then crawl. <</dialog>> <<updateobjective "day_2" "Use the pit to escape the goblins and get out of the mine">> <<changestat "health" -40>> <<changestat "energy" -15>> [[Crawl to Freedom|day_2_15]]She got under my arm, her shoulder against my ribs, and heaved me up the side of the pit. Half-elf strength leaner, denser muscle, pound for pound significantly more powerful than human. She carried most of my weight without complaint, though the strain showed in the cords of her neck and the set of her jaw. We made the top. The entrance fifteen paces. Moonlight. The smell of rain-washed air. Freedom. Five more goblins between us and the way out. I looked at Mira. She looked at me. <<dialog "Mira">>You can't fight.<</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">>Watch me.<</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">>You can barely stand.<</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">>I don't need to stand. I need to swing.<</dialog>> She propped me against the tunnel wall. My back to the stone, ruined leg stretched out. Longsword in both hands, blade angled across my body. I couldn't advance, retreat, or maneuver. All I could do was hold the wall and kill anything within reach. Mira picked up her bow. Nocked an arrow. Stepped in front of me. <<dialog "Mira">> Stay behind me and try not to die. I'm not carrying a corpse back to Valdmere. <</dialog>> What followed was the longest two minutes of my life. She fought like something from a battle song. Two arrows into the first goblin before it closed to ten paces both in the chest, the creature staggering back and falling. She dropped the bow, drew the short sword, and met the next two at the tunnel's narrowest point, using the walls to prevent flanking. The cheese sword moved in tight, efficient arcs. Parry, riposte, a lateral cut that opened a goblin's arm to the bone. It dropped its weapon. She finished it through the neck. One got past her. It came from my left, low and fast, cleaver raised. I was sitting against a wall with a destroyed ankle and a perforated calf and a sword that felt like it weighed a thousand pounds. The goblin was small and quick and smiling with all forty-seven of its horrible teeth. I swung. Not elegant. Not trained. A desperate sweeping cut driven by adrenaline and the absolute refusal to die in a goblin mine sitting in filthy water. The blade caught the creature across the midsection and kept going, powered by terror, cutting deep enough that I felt the edge scrape against its spine. The goblin fell in two directions at once. One left. The big one. Broader than the rest, thick, crude metal armor hammered onto its shoulders, a helmet made from what looked like a human skull with the top sawn off. A leader. A sergeant. The kind others followed because it was meaner and uglier and harder to kill. It came straight at me. Not at Mira at me. The injured prey. The one who couldn't run. Predator logic. Mira put an arrow in its shoulder. It didn't slow down. <img src="img/scene/day_2/19.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> I brought my longsword up. The goblin sergeant's blade a proper short sword, looted from the caravan came in hard and fast, diagonal slash aimed at my neck. I parried. The impact rattled my arms to the shoulders. This thing was strong not human-strong, but wiry, dense, with the cornered-animal power that compensated for size. Our blades locked. It leaned in, pressing weight against my sword, trying to slide its edge to my hands. Its breath hit my face warm, rancid, raw meat and pipe fungus. I headbutted it. My forehead cracked against the bridge of its nose goblins had surprisingly solid noses, dense cartilage over thin bone and it staggered back, green-black blood spurting from its nostrils. Not much room. But enough. I thrust. The longsword went in under the crude armor, between the ribs, and found something vital. The goblin sergeant made a sound quiet, almost surprised, like someone told unexpected news and folded forward over my blade. Twist. Withdraw. It fell. Silence. The tunnel quiet except for my ragged breathing and the drip of water and blood. Mira stood over me. Short sword dripping. Chest heaving. She looked down the tunnel toward the camp. Nothing coming. <<dialog "Mira">> Can you move? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Not well. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Good enough. <</dialog>> She hauled me up. One arm over her shoulder, most of my weight on her, my ruined leg dragging. We limped to the entrance. Past the sentry's rock empty now, the alarm-blower long gone. Into the rain-washed air of the forest. I'd never loved the smell of rain more in my entire life. <<updateobjective "day_2" "Escape the mine and get back to Valdmere">> <<changestat "health" -20>> <<changestat "energy" -20>> [[Go Outside|day_2_16]]<<set $mcLocation = "mine_entrance">> <img src="img/scene/day_2/20.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Fifty paces out. I told her to stop. The pain in my ankle had settled into a constant throbbing heat spreading up my leg. The calf wound was bleeding again the makeshift bandage she'd tied from a strip of her own sleeve was soaked through. She lowered me against a tree trunk. Pulled my boot off both of us working it, her pulling, me biting a leather strap, and when it came free the relief and agony arrived simultaneously. My ankle was twice its normal size. Deep purple-blue, visible even by moonlight. She probed with her fingers and I gripped tree roots hard enough to leave nail marks. <<dialog "Mira">> Not broken. Badly sprained. Maybe a torn ligament. The calf is worse. <</dialog>> She unwrapped the bandage. The splinter wound was ugly a ragged puncture in the meat of the muscle, deep enough that the edges gaped. Something still in there. I could feel it foreign body, rotten timber fragment, sitting inside my calf like a sliver of malice. <<dialog "Mira">> There's still wood in the wound. I can't get it out here. Not in the dark, not with dirty hands. If it stays in, it'll fester. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Then we find a healer. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> In Valdmere? At this hour? The temple healers won't see you without a donation we can't afford, and the apothecary on Mill Street closes at sunset. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> There has to be someone. <</dialog>> The forest dripped around us. Patient. Indifferent. <<dialog "Mira">> There's someone. In the Undercity. A woman I've heard about. She operates out of the old cistern district near the Lowgate. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You've HEARD about her. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> From other sellswords. People who get hurt at inconvenient hours and can't afford temple prices. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What kind of healer operates out of a cistern at midnight? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The kind who doesn't ask questions and doesn't charge much. Her name is Ysolde. They call her the Cistern Witch. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That's not reassuring. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> No one calls her that to her face. Listen to me. <</dialog>> She crouched in front of me, her amber eyes catching the moonlight. <<dialog "Mira">> You've got a piece of rotten wood buried in your calf. If we wait until morning, you'll have an infection. A bad one. The kind that takes legs. I've seen it happen twice. First man lost the leg at the knee. Second man lost it at the hip, and then lost the rest of himself three days later. <</dialog>> I looked at my leg. The swelling getting worse. The wound edges hot unnaturally hot. <<dialog "Aldric">> Fine. The Cistern Witch. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Ysolde. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Whatever. Take me there. <</dialog>> <<set $day_2_17 = false>> <<link "Get Back to Valdmere, Cistern district">> <<worldmap>> <</link>><<set $day_2_17 = true>> Getting back to Valdmere took three times as long as getting out. Mira half-carried me through the dark forest my arm over her shoulder, her arm around my waist, both of us stumbling like the world's worst three-legged race. My leg throbbed with every step. The bleeding left a trail of dark drops on wet leaves behind us. We entered through the south gate. River side. Fewer guards. Cheaper bribes. Mira dropped a copper into the night guard's hand without breaking stride. He looked away with the practiced disinterest of a man who'd seen worse. <img src="img/scene/day_2/21.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> The Undercity was different at night than during the morning's market run. Not safer, not more dangerous, just different the way a forest is different at night, the same geography rearranged by shadow and silence. The narrow streets felt like throats. The leaning buildings like conspirators. Water seeped up through cobblestone cracks. The cistern district was the lowest point of the Undercity. The old stone cisterns the city's ancient water supply, drained and sealed centuries ago sat under sagging buildings that shifted as the ground slowly settled. The streets here were perpetually damp. The air tasted of mineral and mold. Mira stopped in front of a door. <img src="img/scene/day_2/22.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Unremarkable. Wooden. Weathered. Set into stone between a shuttered chandler's shop and a building that smelled of fermenting something. No sign. No marking. Just a door. <<set $day_2_18 = false>> <<updateobjective "day_2" "Find Ysolde, the Cistern Witch, and get her to treat your leg">> [[Knock on the door|CisternDistrict]]<<set $day_2_18 = true>> She knocked. Three times, then twice, then once. Silence. Then footsteps soft, measured, unhurried. A bolt. A chain. The door opened inward. The woman standing in the doorway was not what I expected. I'd been picturing a cistern witch. Hunched. Warted. The kind who'd have a black cat and a cauldron and would cackle at inappropriate moments. Ysolde was none of those things. <img src="img/scene/day_2/23.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> She was tall nearly my height and thin, with the angular, austere beauty of a woman who'd been striking in youth and had hardened into something more interesting with age. Fifty, maybe older. Iron-gray hair pulled back in a severe braid over one shoulder. Eyes so dark that in the lamplight, iris disappeared into pupil. They moved over me with the quick assessing gaze of someone who saw injured bodies so regularly the diagnosis was happening before I opened my mouth. Simple linen dress under a leather apron stained with things I didn't want to identify. Hands long-fingered, steady, surprisingly elegant hanging at her sides and on her left wrist, a bracelet of small glass vials, each containing a different colored liquid. They clinked softly when she moved, like tiny wind chimes. <<dialog "Ysolde">> The leg. <</dialog>> Not a question. <<dialog "Mira">> Splinter wound. Deep. There's still wood in the muscle and the ankle sprained, possibly torn. <</dialog>> Ysolde looked at Mira, then at me. Those dark depthless eyes evaluated, calculated, and arrived at a conclusion in the space of a heartbeat. <<dialog "Ysolde">> Bring him in. <</dialog>> <<updateobjective "day_2" "Ysolde has agreed to treat your leg. Go inside her workshop.">> [[Go inside|day_2_19]]<<changestat "health" 10>> <<changestat "energy" 10>> The inside of Ysolde's practice workshop lair was a single large room that had once been a cellar. Stone walls. Low ceiling. The faint sound of water running somewhere beneath the floor. Lit by oil lamps and beeswax candles, the light warm and steady. Shelves lined every wall, packed with glass bottles, ceramic jars, bundles of dried herbs, rolled bandages, instruments ranging from medical to obscure. A heavy wooden table in the center, scarred and stained with decades of use. A smaller table beside it covered in a white cloth, arranged with tools forceps, needles, thread, scissors, and a small bone saw that I very much hoped was decorative. <img src="img/scene/day_2/24.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> The smell was better than expected. Herbs lavender, sage, something sharp and clean that cut through the damp. Professional. Mira helped me onto the central table. Cold wood against my back through damp clothes. Ysolde moved around the room gathering materials basin of water, strips of clean linen, a leather case that unrolled to reveal delicate surgical instruments. <<dialog "Ysolde">> Trousers. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Ysolde">> Remove them. Or I'll cut them off. Your choice. <</dialog>> Mira helped me peel the trousers down over my swollen ankle. The process involved enough suppressed screaming to power a small theatrical production. The calf wound was worse than it had looked in the forest angry red skin, swollen edges, yellowish seepage from the deepest part. Ysolde examined it with her fingers. Firm but not rough. Practiced hands. She pressed around the wound, probing, and I gripped the table edges. <<dialog "Ysolde">> Deep. Approximately two inches of foreign material still embedded. The wood has begun to splinter inside the wound track. This will be unpleasant. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> More unpleasant than getting it was? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Ysolde">> Possibly. <</dialog>> She selected three bottles from the shelf. Clear. Amber and a deep, unsettling green. She poured the clear liquid over the wound first clean antiseptic burn that made me hiss through my teeth. Then she opened the leather case and selected long, thin forceps. <<dialog "Ysolde">> Hold still and try not to scream. My neighbors are already irritated with me. <</dialog>> The extraction took ten minutes. It felt like ten hours. She worked with meticulous precision, forceps probing the wound track, finding fragments of rotten timber buried in my calf muscle and withdrawing them one by one. Eight pieces. From matchstick-size to a splinter the length of my little finger that came out trailing a dark streamer of blood. I held still. I did not scream. I may have whispered words that would have gotten me banned from every temple in the city, but I did not scream. When the last fragment came out, she irrigated again with the clear liquid, then applied the amber solution warm, viscous, with a numbing quality that spread through the wounded tissue like a blessing. The pain didn't disappear. It retreated. Screaming foreground to dull distant throb. She stitched the wound closed. Twelve neat sutures, each placed with the care of a seamstress on a wedding dress. Wrapped it in clean linen, firm but not tight. The ankle got a different treatment. She manipulated the joint testing range of motion, pressing specific points that made me wince and one that nearly launched me off the table. Then a poultice green, foul-smelling packed around the swollen joint and wrapped in place. <<dialog "Ysolde">> Severe sprain. Partial ligament tear. Two to three weeks if you stay off it. If you insist on walking, wrap tightly and use a staff. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The calf? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Ysolde">> The infection risk is the concern. The wood was rotten. Old mine timber. Full of microbial contamination. <</dialog>> She turned to the shelf and selected a small glass vial. The green one.
