My body moved the way it always moved heavy, solid, the predictable machinery of a man who'd been swinging a sword since he was sixteen and carrying everything he owned on his back since nineteen. Broad shoulders, thick arms, the working muscle of a sellsword who couldn't afford a training hall and didn't need one because the world was his training hall and it charged admission in blood and bruises. I stood, stretched, and felt my spine crack in three places. Twenty-six years old. Felt like forty on mornings like this. Mira pocketed the nine coppers all of them, which I noted but didn't challenge because she was better with money than I was, which was like saying a fish was better at swimming than a stone and stood. She was already dressed. She was always already dressed. In three months of sharing beds and roads and everything in between, I'd learned that Mira woke before dawn by instinct, dressed in the dark by habit, and had assessed every threat and opportunity within a hundred paces before I'd finished blinking the sleep from my eyes. Half-elf metabolism. Leaner, faster, more efficient than human in every measurable way. It was annoying as hell. <<dialog "Aldric">> We'll figure something out. We always do. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We always figure something out because one of us is a relentless optimist and the other one actually makes plans. Guess which one you are. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The handsome one? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Put your trousers on, handsome. We're going downstairs before the bread gets any staler. <</dialog>> <<addobjective "day_1" "Go downstairs for Breakfast">> [[Go downstairs for Breakfast|broken_antler]]<<set $day_1_2 = true>> <<changestat "energy" 10>> Breakfast was exactly as bad as predicted. The common room of the Broken Antler was the architectural equivalent of a sigh low ceilings stained brown with decades of pipe smoke, furniture that had been repaired so many times it was more nail than wood, a floor that stuck to your boots in ways that demanded you not investigate the cause. The hearth was cold. The windows were grimy. The innkeeper a heavyset man with the conversational range of a brick stood behind the bar doing something to his ledger that might have been arithmetic or might have been doodling. Hard to tell. Hard to care. He set two plates in front of us without being asked. Stale bread, hard cheese, two cups of the house ale. The bread had the consistency of a cobblestone's friendlier cousin. The cheese had achieved the kind of hardness that suggested it had ambitions of becoming furniture. The ale tasted like guilt dissolved in rainwater. I ate. You don't get picky when you're broke. Mira picked at the bread with her fingers, tearing it into small pieces and eating them one at a time. In her other hand, the arrowhead one of her broadheads, wicked-looking thing with three razor edges which she used to pick her teeth between bites. Click. Click. Click. The sound of the metal against her canines set my nerves on edge the same way it had since Thornwall, which was to say, constantly, persistently, and with the grim reliability of sunrise. <<dialog "Aldric">> Must you? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Must I what? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The teeth thing. With the arrow. It sounds like a tiny blacksmith working on a tiny anvil inside your mouth. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It helps me think. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> About what? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> About how we're going to avoid sleeping next to a pile of fish intestines tomorrow night. Unless you'd prefer I stop thinking about that. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Think away. <</dialog>> <img src="img/scene/day_1/2.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Click. Click. Click. I drank the terrible ale and stared at the rain-streaked shutters. Outside, Valdmere was doing what Valdmere always did in autumn drowning. It had been raining for two days straight, the kind of cold, relentless downpour that found every crack in your boots and every gap in your collar and settled into your bones like a tenant who'd lost the deposit and didn't care. The cobblestones would be rivers. The market stalls would be shuttered. The whole city would be wrapped in a wet gray misery that matched the wet gray misery sitting in my chest. <<dialog "Mira">> We have options. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Let's hear them. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Day labor at the docks. They always need muscle to load cargo ships, especially in rain when the regular workers call in sick. Pays about three coppers a day. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Three coppers won't cover the room. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I said we have options. I didn't say they were good options. Second, the mercenary board at the garrison. There might be something posted since last week. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Last week it was rat-clearing and escort jobs that paid in soup. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Third option, we pawn something. <</dialog>> That landed on the table between us like a dead bird. We both looked at our weapons my longsword leaning against the wall, her bow in its oilskin case beside the bed upstairs. The tools of our trade. The only things of value we owned. <<dialog "Aldric">> My sword might fetch five silver. If the pawnbroker's feeling generous, which pawnbrokers never are. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> My bow is worth thirty. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You'd sooner cut off your hand. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'd sooner cut off YOUR hand. My hand I need for the bow. Which I'm not pawning. So that option is dead. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Then we're back to dock labor and the garrison board. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We're back to dock labor and the garrison board. <</dialog>> She put the arrowhead away. When Mira stopped picking her teeth, it meant she'd finished thinking and had arrived at a conclusion. The conclusion, from the set of her jaw and the flatness of her amber eyes, was not one that made her happy. <<dialog "Mira">> Let's try the garrison first. If there's nothing, we haul cargo in the rain and hate ourselves for it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Sounds like a plan. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It sounds like desperation with a schedule. But it's what we've got. <</dialog>> <<set $day_1_3 = false>> <<updateobjective "day_1" "Check the garrison board for mercenary work">> <<link "Go to the garrison board at east garrison">> <<regionmap "valdmere">> <</link>><<set $mcLocation = "east_garrison">> <<set $day_1_3 = true>> The east garrison mercenary board was a slab of weathered oak nailed to the wall beside the guardhouse, protected from the rain by an overhang that didn't quite do its job. Half the postings were water-damaged, the ink bleeding into illegibility. The other half were legible and depressing. I stood in front of it, rain dripping off the brim of my hood, and read each one with the desperate optimism of a man looking for a diamond in a pile of horse manure. <img src="img/scene/day_1/3.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> <<dialog "Aldric">> Rat-clearing. Three coppers, bring your own poison. Same posting from last week. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Next. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Escort contract merchant family heading north. Payment in meals and lodging, no coin. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We can't eat lodging. Next. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Bounty on a pickpocket. Two silver. Been posted for three weeks. Either the pickpocket is very good or two silver isn't worth the effort. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Both. Next. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That's it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> That can't be it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> There's one more, but it's asking for a wizard and I checked this morning I'm still not a wizard. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Have you tried? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Tried what? Being a wizard? You don't just try being a wizard, Mira. It requires years of training and a fundamental connection to the arcane that <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I meant have you tried reading the fine print. Sometimes wizard-required postings accept armed escort as a substitute if the client is desperate enough. <</dialog>> I leaned closer. Squinted through the rain at the smudged text. The client wanted a wizard to clear a haunted cellar. Specifically, the ghost of a cat that was scaring the household staff. Payment, one silver and a basket of turnips. <<dialog "Aldric">> It's a ghost cat. For turnips. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I hate this city. <</dialog>> We left the garrison. The rain was still falling. Valdmere was between conflicts the border dispute with the northern provinces had settled, the pirate activity off the coast had been quelled by a naval expedition last month, and the internal guild wars had reached a temporary truce that left everyone armed and unemployed. The mercenary market was flooded with idle swords, and the pay had cratered to the point where honest labor at the docks was starting to look competitive. We walked through the market district because it was on the way back and because sometimes walking past things you can't afford is its own kind of entertainment. The stalls were half-shuttered against the rain, their awnings sagging with pooled water, the merchants huddled under them like refugees from joy. Mira stopped at a fletcher's stall. The fletcher a lean, sun-browned woman with arms like braided rope had her wares displayed under a waxed canvas tent, arrows, bowstrings, quivers, a pair of hand-carved crossbow bolts that were more art than weapon. <img src="img/scene/day_1/4.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> <<dialog "Mira">> Look at that bowstring. <</dialog>> She said it the way another woman might say "look at that necklace" or "look at that dress." With longing. With the hungry reverence of someone who appreciated the craft behind the object. The bowstring was silk-and-sinew blend, treated with something that gave it a faint luster even in the gray light. Professional grade. The kind of string that turned a good bow into a great one. <<dialog "Aldric">> How much? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> More than nine coppers. Don't ask. <</dialog>> She walked away. Didn't look back. I filed it away the way she'd looked at the bowstring, the particular angle of her chin when she'd forced herself to move on. If we ever had money again, I'd come back and buy it for her. I wouldn't tell her I was doing it. She'd punch me for being sentimental and then she'd string her bow with it and never mention it again, and that would be her way of saying thank you. Two stalls down, a blacksmith was repairing a sword with a technique I'd never seen folding the heated metal at an angle that shouldn't have worked but somehow did, the hammer strikes producing a tone like a bell rather than the usual dull ring. I stopped to watch. The rhythm was hypnotic. Strike, fold, strike, turn, strike, fold. The metal glowed cherry-red under the rain, steam rising from the anvil in thin white ghosts. <img src="img/scene/day_1/5.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Ten minutes passed. The blade took shape a short sword, curved slightly, with a single edge and a fuller groove that would make it whistle when swung. Beautiful work. The kind of craft that separated a smith who made swords from a smith who made weapons. <<dialog "Mira">> Are you going to stand here all day watching a man hit metal? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> He's not just hitting metal. Look at the fold angle that's a northern technique. You don't see that this far south. The grain structure will be <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Aldric. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We are broke. We are homeless as of tomorrow. I love that you appreciate craftsmanship. I do. It's charming. But if I stand in this rain for one more minute watching you watch a blacksmith, I am going to take that glowing sword and insert it somewhere creative. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Fine. We're going. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We're going. <</dialog>> We went. But I looked back once. The smith caught my eye and gave me a nod one craftsman to another, even though my craft was using the blade rather than making it. I nodded back. Nice moment. Didn't pay the rent. On the way back, Mira suggested we spend two coppers on decent ale from a proper taproom rather than the Broken Antler's liquid punishment. <<dialog "Aldric">> We could. Two coppers for something that actually tastes like ale instead of like regret. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Or we save the two coppers and drink regret at the Antler for free. Since we're already paying for the room. <</dialog>> We looked at each other. The rain dripped off our hoods. A cart rolled past, splashing mud across both our boots. Somewhere nearby, a dog barked at nothing. <<dialog "Aldric">> Save it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Save it. <</dialog>> We walked back to the Broken Antler in silence. Sometimes saving two coppers feels like winning. Most of the time it just feels like being poor. <<nobr>> <<set $barmaid_done = false>> <<set $arm_wrestler_done = false>> <<set $day_1_4 = false>> <<set $board_sergeant_start = false>> <<addsidequest "barmaids_eye" "The Barmaid's Eye" "Talk with Her">> <<addsidequest "arm_wrestler" "The Arm Wrestler" "Challenge Him">> <</nobr>> <<updateobjective "day_1" "Go back to the Broken Antler">> <<link "Walk back to the Broken Antler">> <<regionmap "valdmere">> <</link>><<set $mcLocation = "broken_antler">> The common room was emptier in the afternoon. A few day-drinkers nursing their tankards like the ale might run away if they let go. The old man in the corner the one who'd been there every single day since we arrived, asleep with a fat orange cat on his chest, both of them breathing in synchronized wheezes was still there. Still asleep. The cat opened one eye when we walked in, judged us, and closed it again. I ordered two of the terrible house ales. Three coppers each. Six total. That left us three coppers to our name. Three coppers between two armed professionals who'd been traveling together for three months and had somehow managed to spend every coin they earned faster than they earned it. My father would have been proud. He'd been a master of the same trick, back before the lord took the farm and the drink took him. Mira settled into our corner booth the one with the high-backed seats that let us keep our backs to the wall and our eyes on the door. Old habit. Professional paranoia. She arranged herself the way she always did, bow case under the table within reach, short sword at her hip, a clear line of sight to both exits. <<dialog "Mira">> We need to think differently. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Differently how? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The garrison board is dead. The docks pay pennies. We're not pawning weapons. So we need a different channel. Private contracts. Under-the-table work. The kind of jobs that don't get posted on public boards because the people offering them don't want public attention. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You're talking about the kind of work that gets you stabbed in an alley. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm talking about the kind of work that pays in silver instead of turnips. There's a difference. Slim difference, admittedly. But present. <</dialog>> I drank my ale. Tasted like defeat with a frothy head. The common room was dim, the afternoon light barely making it through the grimy windows. Rain hammered the shutters in irregular bursts, each one a reminder that the world outside was wet and cold and not interested in our problems. That's when I noticed the board. Not the garrison board a different one. Smaller, nailed to the wall near the bar, half-hidden behind a hanging lamp that hadn't been lit. I'd walked past it every day for five days and never looked closely. Tavern-specific postings. Local noise. Lost items, rooms for let, a notice about a missing tabby cat that was probably living with the old man in the corner based on the description. But one card stood out. Hand-lettered on thick parchment, the kind of paper that cost money, which meant whoever wrote it had some. The ink was dark, the letters precise. <<set $check_card_1 = false>> <<set $day_1_4 = true>> <<updateobjective "day_1" "Check the card on the tavern board">> [[Check the Card|broken_antler]]<<set $check_card_1 = true>> <span style="color: red;">Discrete procurement services inquire at bar.</span> <img src="img/scene/day_1/6.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> I stared at it. "Discrete procurement services" could mean anything from fetching a noble's lost jewelry to smuggling contraband through the harbor gates. The vagueness was deliberate. The kind of posting that filtered out people who needed too many details before committing. I flagged down the innkeeper. He looked up from his ledger with the enthusiasm of a man being asked to do anything at all. <<dialog "Aldric">> That card on the board. The procurement services. Who posted it? <</dialog>> The innkeeper shrugged a minimal movement involving exactly one shoulder and zero additional effort. <<dialog "Innkeeper">> Man comes in most evenings. Big fellow. Scarred up. Sits at the back, waits for people to ask about the card. Been doing it for about a week. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What kind of work? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Innkeeper">> The kind I don't ask about. That's the kind of tavern this is. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What time does he usually come in? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Innkeeper">> Sunset. Give or take. Orders whiskey, sits, waits. Sometimes people talk to him. Sometimes they don't. Either way, he drinks his whiskey and leaves. <</dialog>> He went back to his ledger. Conversation over. I returned to the booth and told Mira. <<dialog "Mira">> Discrete procurement services. That's a smuggling job. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Or a recovery job. Or a delivery job. Or an assassination, I suppose, if we're being thorough about the possibilities. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We don't do assassinations. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I know we don't do assassinations. I'm listing options. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Well, stop listing that one. What time did the innkeeper say? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Sunset. We wait? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> We wait. <</dialog>> She picked up her arrowhead. Click. Click. Click. Thinking again. I drank my ale and watched the rain and tried to calculate how many hours of terrible ale I could stretch three coppers across. The answer was, not enough. <<updateobjective "day_1" "Wait for sunset">> <<link "Wait for sunset">> <<goto "day_1_5">> <</link>>Sunset in Valdmere was less an event and more a negotiation. The sun didn't so much set as give up, the gray sky darkening by degrees until the lamplighters came out with their poles and the city shifted from daytime misery to nighttime misery with marginally better lighting. The Broken Antler's evening crowd filtered in. Dock workers with calloused hands and hollow eyes, looking for the particular kind of oblivion that three-copper ale provided. A pair of off-duty city guards sharing a pitcher and trading complaints about their sergeant. A group of merchants' apprentices young, loud, soft-handed occupying a table near the hearth and laughing at things that weren't funny. The fire popped and crackled, throwing warm shadows across the low ceiling and making the common room almost bearable if you squinted hard enough and drank fast enough. Mira had switched to water an hour ago. I was on my second ale and beginning to regret spending the copper. The common room smelled like pipe smoke, wet wool, and the particular funk of twenty human bodies crammed into a space designed for ten. The cat on the old man's chest had relocated to the bar, where it sat washing itself with the serene indifference of a creature that had never worried about money in its life. The door opened. The sound of the storm rushed in wind, rain, the distant clatter of cart wheels on wet cobblestones and with it came a man who matched the innkeeper's description the way a landslide matches the word "inconvenient." Wide as a wardrobe. Face that was mostly scar tissue, the kind of face that suggested he'd lost a fight with a cheese grater and won the rematch by eating it. Heavy jaw. Small eyes that moved fast and missed nothing. An oilskin cloak that pooled water on the floor as he crossed the threshold. <img src="img/scene/day_1/7.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Mira's elbow found my ribs. She didn't look at me. Didn't need to. <<dialog "Mira">> That's him. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You think? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Big. Scarred. Oilskin. Ordering whiskey. Either that's our man or the innkeeper's description applies to half the muscle in Valdmere. <</dialog>> The man Grent, presumably collected his whiskey from the bar, exchanged exactly zero words with the innkeeper, and moved to a table at the back of the room. He sat with his shoulders to the wall and his eyes on the door. The same instinct Mira and I had. Professional paranoia recognizes its own kind. He didn't look at us. Didn't look at anyone. He drank his whiskey with the patient stillness of a man who'd done this every evening for a week and would do it every evening for a week more if necessary. A man who understood that the right kind of work found the right kind of people, and the right kind of people were the ones desperate enough to approach a stranger in a tavern based on a card with three vague words on it. I looked at Mira. She looked at our three coppers. <<dialog "Mira">> Well? You going to sit here until we can't afford to sit here anymore? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I was hoping you'd go. You're more intimidating. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm an archer. You're the one with the sword and the jaw. Go sell us. <</dialog>> <<set $grent_1 = false>> <<updateobjective "day_1" "Approch Grent about the card">> [[Approch Grent about the card|broken_antler]]<<set $grent_1 = true>> I picked up my ale mostly for something to do with my hands and crossed the common room. The man watched me approach. Not with alarm, not with welcome. With the flat, evaluating attention of someone who assessed threats and opportunities through the same lens. I sat down across from him without waiting for an invitation. If he wanted people to approach him about that card, he could tolerate the lack of ceremony. <<dialog "Aldric">> Saw your card on the board. Discrete procurement services. I'm here to ask about it. <</dialog>> He looked at me. Then past me, at Mira in our corner booth the bow case visible under the table, the short sword at her hip, the particular coiled readiness of someone who could kill you from fifty paces and was mildly annoyed about being alive. <<dialog "Grent">> Name's Grent. Merchant Consortium, Valdmere chapter. You two sellswords? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm a sellsword. She's an archer. She'll tell you there's a difference. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Same thing with extra steps. Bring her over. <</dialog>> I waved Mira across. She came unhurried, ale in hand, settling into the chair beside me with the deliberate ease of someone who wanted you to know she was armed and comfortable and not particularly impressed by you. Grent watched her sit with the same flat appraisal he'd given me. Then he reached inside his oilskin cloak, produced a folded parchment, and placed it on the table between us with the precise, deliberate placement of a man laying down a card he knew would change the game. <<dialog "Grent">> Got a contract. Night work. Twenty silver each, half up front. <</dialog>> Twenty silver. The number hit me like a physical force. Twenty silver was a month of rooms and meals. It was new boots and a proper sharpening stone and ale that didn't taste like someone's worst memory. It was the difference between sleeping on a bed and sleeping on a pile of fish guts. My hand was reaching for the parchment before my brain finished processing, the instinct of a man who'd been broke long enough that money had its own gravitational pull. Under the table, Mira kicked me. Hard. Right in the shin. The universal signal for don't look desperate, you idiot. I pulled my hand back. But I could see the number working behind her eyes too those amber half-elf eyes doing the same math mine were doing, calculating room costs and food budgets and how far twenty silver could stretch if you spent it carefully. Neither of us spent anything carefully. But it was nice to imagine. <<dialog "Mira">> What kind of night work? <</dialog>> <img src="img/scene/day_1/8.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Grent leaned back. The chair creaked under him like a ship in heavy seas. <<dialog "Grent">> Supply caravan got hit three days ago on the Ashenmoor Road. Four leagues east, give or take. Whole wagon of alchemical reagents sealed crates, specialty goods. Valuable stuff. The guards were killed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> By what? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Goblins. Warband operating out of the old Greymire mine. Scouts put them at fifteen, maybe twenty strong. Been hitting shipments for weeks grab and run, nothing organized. The Consortium wants the cargo recovered. Whatever's still intact. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Fifteen to twenty goblins. In a mine. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Small goblins. Big mine. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> There's no such thing as a small goblin when you're underground with fifteen of them. They fight dirty, they know the terrain, and they have the kind of morale that comes from being too stupid to be afraid. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Which is why I'm paying twenty silver each and not five. The Consortium is aware that this job carries risk. We're also aware that the cargo sitting in that mine is worth considerably more than forty silver, which means your compensation is generous but not unreasonable. Think of it as a fair exchange your skills and your risk tolerance for our money and our problem. <</dialog>> Mira's arrowhead came out. She held it between two fingers, turning it slowly, the broadhead catching the firelight. Click against her thumbnail. Click. Click. Her thinking tell. Grent watched the arrowhead with the careful attention of a man who recognized a weapon when he saw one, even a small one being used for dental hygiene. <<dialog "Mira">> What's in the crates? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Sealed alchemical reagents. Specialty compounds for clients who pay premium rates and prefer discretion. The specifics are above your pay grade and below your interest, unless you're planning to open an apothecary. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm planning to not get killed by something that leaks out of a broken crate while I'm carrying it through a goblin-infested tunnel in the dark. What kind of reagents? Volatile? Toxic? Corrosive? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Some of all three. Which is why the sealed crates matter and the broken ones don't. If a seal's intact, the contents are stable. If a seal's broken, leave it. Don't open them. Don't drink them. Don't sniff them. Some of that stuff is meant for controlled application by trained alchemists, and the results of uncontrolled exposure range from unpleasant to fatal, with several creative stops in between. <</dialog>> He shrugged a gesture that involved so much shoulder it was practically a geological event. The oilskin cloak rustled like a tent in a gale. <<dialog "Grent">> Twenty silver each guaranteed. Plus a two-silver bonus per sealed crate you bring back. The Consortium doesn't expect all of it. Just whatever you can carry. <</dialog>> I looked at Mira. She looked at my nine coppers sitting on the table next to the ale tankards, a tiny monument to our failure as functional adults. She looked at the folded parchment with the Consortium seal. She looked at me. The conversation happened in the space between her blinks. Her: This is dangerous. Me: Everything we do is dangerous. Her: Underground. Close quarters. My bow is useless in a tunnel. Me: You have the short sword. Her: I hate that sword. Me: Twenty silver. Her: ... Twenty silver. She put the arrowhead away. <<dialog "Mira">> When? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Tonight, if you're smart. Tomorrow at the latest. The longer those crates sit in a goblin nest, the less likely anything inside them survives. Goblins are curious creatures. They poke things. They taste things. Eventually they break things. The window for recovery narrows every hour. <</dialog>> I picked up the parchment. The Consortium seal was pressed into the wax a pair of scales over a ship's wheel, the universal symbol of people who had money and wanted more of it. The contract was straightforward. Recover sealed cargo from the Greymire mine. Return to Consortium warehouse on Dockside Row. Ask for a woman named Voss. She'd handle payment. <<dialog "Aldric">> We'll go tonight. <</dialog>> Under the table, Mira kicked me again. Harder this time. I was going to have a bruise the shape of her boot heel on my shin for a week. <<dialog "Aldric">> Sorry, We'll go tomorrow night. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Grent">> Good. Half up front. <</dialog>> He produced a small leather pouch from inside his oilskin cloak and counted out twenty silver coins on the table. The sound they made that particular music, that bright metallic chime of real money hitting wood was the most beautiful noise I'd heard in weeks. Maybe months. Each coin caught the firelight as it landed, winking like a tiny promise. Grent divided them into two piles. Ten and ten. He pushed one toward me, one toward Mira. I picked mine up and the weight of them warm from his pocket, solid, real settled against my palm like an answer to a prayer I'd been too proud to say. <<dialog "Grent">> You get the rest plus bonuses when you deliver the crates. Dockside Row. Voss. She's thorough, so have the cargo count ready. <</dialog>> He stood. Reached into his cloak and pulled out a thick charcoal pencil and the napkin from under his whiskey glass. He spread the napkin flat and began sketching quick, sure lines, the practiced hand of a man who'd drawn tactical maps on worse surfaces. <<dialog "Grent">> Upper tunnels branch off the main shaft about fifty paces in. The camp is here central chamber, old crew quarters. This is where they'll be sleeping. The storage shafts angle down from a junction point here. <</dialog>> He jabbed a thick finger at the napkin. document.getElementById('board_sergeant_start'); if (e) e.remove(); } }, 0); >><<set $arm_wrestler_done = true>> The noise started around the third round of terrible ale. Not the usual tavern noise the ambient soup of conversation and coughing and furniture creaking that was the Broken Antler's default soundtrack. This was different. Focused. The concentrated buzz of people gathering around something interesting, which was remarkable because nothing interesting had happened in the Broken Antler since the founding of the monarchy and possibly before that. I looked up from my tankard. The corner table the big one, scarred and ring-stained, usually occupied by a rotating cast of sullen dock workers had drawn a crowd. Six, seven people, pressing close, leaning in, the particular posture of spectators at a contest. Coin glinted on the table. Someone laughed. Someone else groaned. <<dialog "Mira">> Arm wrestling. <</dialog>> She said it the way she said most things flatly, with just enough inflection to communicate that she'd already assessed the situation, found it beneath her, and was tolerating its existence in her visual field out of sheer generosity. <<dialog "Aldric">> How can you tell from here? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The rhythm. Listen. Crowd goes quiet that's the grip. Low murmur that's the push. Then either cheering or groaning someone wins or loses. It's been cycling for the last twenty minutes. Someone's beating everyone. <</dialog>> I listened. She was right. The pattern was there, rhythmic as breathing silence, murmur, eruption and the eruptions were mostly groans, which meant the same person was winning, which meant someone at that table had arms strong enough to beat every challenger in a working-class tavern, which was saying something because the Broken Antler's clientele was built from dock labor and disappointment, both of which produced considerable forearm development. <<dialog "Mira">> Don't even think about it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm not thinking about anything. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You're thinking about the exact thing I told you not to think about. I can see it. Your right arm just flexed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> That was involuntary. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Your involuntary responses are the most honest thing about you, and they're all saying "I want to arm-wrestle that man." <</dialog>> She wasn't wrong. My right arm had flexed. The forearm, specifically the thick cable of muscle running from elbow to wrist that seven years of daily swordwork had built into the most reliable piece of equipment I owned. It had flexed at the sound of competition the way a dog's ears prick at the sound of a whistle. Muscle memory. Reflex. The body saying yes before the brain had finished thinking maybe. I stood up. <<dialog "Mira">> Aldric <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm just going to look. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> That's what you said about the dwarf in Kestwick. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I looked and then I arm-wrestled the dwarf. My shoulder clicked for a month. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You want to do this again because...? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Because I'm down to few coppers and there's coin on that table. <</dialog>> She opened her mouth. Closed it. The math was undeniable we were broke, and the pile of silver glinting under the corner lamp was more money than we'd seen collectively in two weeks. Mira was pragmatic above all things, and pragmatism had a hard time arguing against eight silver when the alternative was porridge and misery. <<dialog "Mira">> If your shoulder clicks again, I'm not massaging it out this time. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You said that about Kestwick. You massaged it out three times. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I was in a generous mood. I'm not in a generous mood. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You're never in a generous mood. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Yet here I am. Following you toward another bad decision. There's probably a lesson in that. <</dialog>> [[Go towards table|arm_wrestler_brokk]]The crowd parted for me the way crowds always parted for a man with a sword on his hip, even in a place where swords were common currency. Not out of respect. Out of the instinct that said this one might be next and I want a good viewing angle and then I saw Brokk. He sat at the corner table like a mountain sits in a valley immovably, inevitably, with the casual certainty of a geological feature that had been there since before the surrounding landscape was relevant. Early twenties. Built like someone had taken a normal human body and hired a second crew to add more of everything. Arms like bridge cables. Shoulders that could have supported a load-bearing wall. A neck that started at his jaw and ended at his collarbones without the usual courtesy of narrowing in between. His hands gods, his hands were the size of dinner plates, each finger thick as a sausage, the palms calloused to the texture of old leather. He was a blacksmith's apprentice. I didn't need to be told the burns on his forearms said it, the soot embedded in his knuckle creases said it, the particular development of his deltoids and triceps said it. Forge work. Hammer work. The monotonous, beautiful brutality of heating metal and hitting it until it became something useful. His body was the biography of his trade, written in muscle and scar tissue. He'd beaten four challengers. They sat around the table in various states of defeat nursing ales, flexing sore wrists, wearing the particular expression of men whose masculinity had been readjusted by a man half their age. The pot on the table had grown to eight silver in mixed coin, contributed by the losers and augmented by side bets from the crowd. Brokk saw me looking. He grinned. Not a smirk a genuine, uncomplicated grin. The grin of a young man who was very good at one specific thing and took pure, uncynical pleasure in being good at it. No malice. No posturing. Just the simple delight of a body doing what it was built for. <<dialog "Brokk">> You look like you've got arms under that tunic. Want to test them? <</dialog>> His voice was surprisingly light for his size a clear, carrying tenor that didn't match the bass rumble you'd expect from a man built like a fortification. Young. Cheerful. The voice of someone who hadn't yet learned that the world was going to ask more from him than physical strength, and who wouldn't believe it if you told him. <<dialog "Aldric">> What's the buy-in? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Brokk">> Two silver to sit. Winner takes the pot. Eight silver and change more than you'd make in a week of honest work, assuming you do honest work, which with that sword I'm guessing you don't. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I do very honest work. People pay me to solve problems. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Brokk">> What of the sword? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Some problems don't respond to polite conversation. <</dialog>> Brokk laughed. A big, room-filling laugh, the kind that came from a chest that could have served as a resonating chamber for a cathedral bell. Several people in the crowd smiled reflexively laughter that genuine was contagious, a biological response to unfiltered joy. <<dialog "Brokk">> I like you. Sit down, sellsword. Let's see what you've got. <</dialog>> Mira materialized at my shoulder. I hadn't heard her approach I never did, half-elf silence being what it was but I felt her presence the way you feel a change in the weather. A hand on my arm. Light. Fingers barely touching the fabric. <<dialog "Mira">> Two silver is everything we have left after the room. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I know. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> If you lose, we can't eat. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Then I'd better not lose. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> That's not a strategy. That's an aspiration. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> All my strategies are aspirations. It's worked out so far. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It has emphatically not worked out so far. We are in this tavern with few coppers because your previous aspirations brought us here. Your aspiration history is a litany of <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Eight silver, Mira. Eight silver and a free ale. When was the last time we had eight silver? <</dialog>> She went quiet. The amber eyes did the math the math she always did, the survival arithmetic that ran underneath everything like a river under cobblestones. Nine coppers. A room paid through one more day. A city that charged three coppers for ale that tasted like grief and on the table, gleaming under lamplight, eight silver coins that represented a month of meals and the breathing room they hadn't had since Thornwall. <<dialog "Mira">> Your shoulder. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Is fine. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> If it clicks <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> It won't click. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> If it clicks, you're useless for a week. We have a contract from Grent. A mine to clear. You need your sword arm. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> My sword arm is my right. I'll wrestle left. <</dialog>> She stared at me. I stared back. The standoff of two people who'd been arguing with each other for three months and had developed the particular efficiency of combatants who knew each other's moves. [[Challenge Brokk|arm_wrestler_challenge]] [[Decline|arm_wrestler_decline]] [[Send Mira|arm_wrestler_send_mira]]I sat down. The chair across from Brokk was warm body heat from the four men who'd sat there before me and lost. The wood of the table was scarred with decades of abuse, the surface a topography of ring-stains and knife-marks and the divots left by countless fists, tankards, and foreheads being driven into it by force or drink. I counted out two silver from my belt pouch and placed them on the table. They joined the pot with a pair of soft clicks that sounded, to my money-starved ears, like a door closing. No going back. Those coins were in the pot now, and they were coming out in my pocket or someone else's. Brokk planted his elbow. The motion was practiced a smooth, mechanical deployment of arm and shoulder onto the table surface, the elbow finding its divot in the wood (he'd been sitting here long enough to wear a depression), the forearm rising vertical, the hand opening like a gate. I planted mine. <<dialog "Brokk">> Good arm. Sword arm? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Both arms. I switch hands depending on the fight. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Brokk">> Fancy. I just hit things until they're the right shape. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Swords or steel? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Brokk">> Both. Though the steel complains less. <</dialog>> I gripped his hand. The contact was immediate and informative, the way shaking a stranger's hand always tells you something but this told you everything. His palm was a slab callused to the texture of boiled leather, hot, dry, the skin so thick over the knuckles that it barely registered pressure. His fingers closed around mine like iron bands not squeezing, not yet, but present. The grip of a man whose hands had been closing around the handles of heavy things since before his voice broke. He could crush walnuts in that grip. He could crush bone. My grip answered. Different vocabulary, same language. Sword-calluses rather than forge-calluses the pads and ridges that formed along the palm and fingers from thousands of hours of gripping a leather-wrapped hilt. My forearm was thick but not massive built for endurance and control rather than raw output, the kind of forearm that could swing a longsword for an hour without cramping because the muscles had been trained to work efficiently rather than explosively. The crowd pressed closer. Bodies around us, warm and ale-scented, the circle tightening like a noose made of spectators. Someone was taking side bets. Someone else was providing commentary in a low, rapid mutter that sounded like an auctioneer describing a horse race. <<dialog "Brokk">> Ready? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Go. <</dialog>> He pushed. The force was there was no other word staggering. Not a burst. Not an explosion. A wave. A slow, mounting, inexorable pressure that came from his shoulder through his arm through his hand through mine and into every tendon, every joint, every fiber of muscle from my wrist to my spine. The man didn't push the way fighters pushed with speed and aggression and the psychology of dominance. He pushed the way gravity pushed. Constantly. Inevitably. Without any interest in whether you were ready for it. My arm bent. One inch. Two. The tendons in my forearm stood out like suspension cables, the veins distending, the skin going white over the knuckles where my grip clamped down in desperate resistance. My shoulder the same shoulder that had clicked for a month after the dwarf in Kestwick screamed a warning that my brain acknowledged and my pride overruled. The first five seconds were assessment. Reading him through the contact the way you read a blade's quality through the vibration of a parry. His strength was massive, unrefined, a raw material that had never been processed into technique. He pushed in a straight line because a straight line was all he'd ever needed. Nobody in this tavern had forced him to do anything else. I shifted my grip. Slightly. A millimeter of repositioning the wrist angling inward, changing the vector, redirecting his force from a direct contest of power into a lever equation where his mass became a liability and my angle became an advantage. A sword technique. The same principle that let a longsword redirect a warhammer's blow you didn't match force, you channeled it. Brokk's eyebrows rose. His arm, which had been pressing mine steadily toward the table, stopped. Not because I'd overpowered him I hadn't, not remotely but because the angle had changed and his straight-line push was suddenly meeting resistance on a diagonal that his muscle memory didn't know how to solve. <<dialog "Brokk">> Oh. That's clever. <</dialog>> He adjusted. Pushed harder. Not just his arm now but his shoulder, his chest, the rotational force of his entire upper body leaning into the contest. The table creaked under the pressure. My arm shook a visible tremor running from elbow to wrist, the muscles fiber-firing in rapid, desperate pulses. The scar on my ribcage pulled tight, the tissue complaining at the strain. My shoulder was making sounds internal sounds, the grinding complaints of a joint being asked to perform at the edge of its tolerance. The crowd had gone silent. The particular silence of people watching something balance on a knife's edge not breathing, not moving, the collective unconscious understanding that the outcome was being decided in this exact second and anything could tip it. I was losing. The math was clear. Brokk was stronger. Objectively, measurably, inarguably stronger his arm was the product of genetics and daily forge work and the simple, unfair advantage of a body built for raw power competing against a body built for endurance. My technique had bought me time. It hadn't bought me victory. My arm was three inches from the table. Two inches. I could feel the wood's proximity like heat the finish line of failure, waiting for my knuckles. I thought about the mine. The contract. The twenty silver that Grent's job would pay. I thought about Mira, watching from behind the crowd, her amber eyes tracking the contest with the precision she applied to everything. I thought about the few coppers in my belt pouch that were all that stood between us and the fish-gutting docks and I thought about my arm. This arm. The thick forearm, the calloused hand, the shoulder that could swing a longsword for an hour, the grip that could hold a blade in rain and blood and fear. My arm. My body. The machine I'd been operating for twenty-six years, the only tool I'd ever truly owned. Something surged. Not technique this time. Not strategy. Just everything. The last reserves. The bottom of the barrel. The place where the body stores the power it doesn't want to use because using it costs something you can't get back. It came from my chest, my gut, the base of my spine, traveling up through the shoulder and down the arm and into the hand and through the grip like lightning through a rod. I pushed. Brokk's arm stopped falling. Held. Quivered at the balance point neither going down nor coming up, both of us locked in a trembling equilibrium that the crowd absorbed with a collective intake of breath. Then, slowly inch by inch, tendon by screaming tendon I pushed him back. His knuckles touched the table with a crack that I felt in my teeth. The crowd erupted. [[Pushed him back|arm_wrestler_victory]]Cheering. Shouting. Someone banging a tankard against the table in rhythmic celebration. The particular, unrestrained roar of a working-class crowd watching an underdog win because that's what I was, apparently, the lean swordsman against the blacksmith mountain, and the lean swordsman had planted the mountain's hand in the wood and the crowd was drunk enough and happy enough to treat it like a minor miracle. I released Brokk's hand. My own was shaking a deep, bone-level tremor that started in the fingers and ran all the way up to the shoulder, the aftershock of muscles that had been asked for everything and had delivered and were now presenting the bill. My forearm felt like someone had run it through a mangle. My shoulder was making clicking sounds. Small ones. Promising to become bigger ones. Brokk leaned back in his chair. He looked at his own hand the hand that had been driven into the table with the expression of a man examining an old friend who'd just done something unexpected. Then he laughed. <<dialog "Brokk">> Ha!
