That was the one constant in an increasingly inconstant world no matter what else changed, the ale at the Antler would always taste like someone had filtered dishwater through an old sock and charged you three coppers for the indignity. I was in the corner booth. Mira was across from me, eating something the menu described as stew and reality described as a warm brown mystery. The common room was in its usual state half-full, all-miserable, the evening crowd filtering in with the slow determination of people who had nowhere better to be. Tess was behind the bar. She brought our drinks tankard for me, tankard for Mira, the automatic delivery of a barmaid who'd memorized her regulars. She set mine down. Her hand paused on the rim. She was looking at me. <img src="img/scene/barmaid/3.png" style="width: 100%; max-width: 768px; margin: 0 auto;" /> Not the casual, reading-the-room glance from before. This was focused. Her eyes quick, sharp, the same eyes that had read my scars in ten seconds were fixed on my face with the particular intensity of someone seeing something that didn't match their records. <<dialog "Tess">> Did you do something different? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Different how? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tess">> You look... I don't know. Rested? Your skin looks good. <</dialog>> My skin. I resisted the urge to touch my face. Resisted the urge to check whether the jawline felt different under my fingers, whether the stubble was thinner, whether any of the changes I'd been trying not to catalogue in front of Mira were visible to someone who hadn't seen me in what? A day? Two? <<dialog "Aldric">> Must be the ale. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tess">> That ale makes everyone look worse, not better. <</dialog>> She laughed. The same quick, warm laugh that crinkled the freckles. But underneath it, her eyes were still working the barmaid's gift, the talent for reading truth in faces, running its analysis against the baseline she'd stored from our first meeting. She'd cataloged me. Filed me and now the file didn't match the face, and the mismatch was nagging at her the way a wrong note nags at a musician. <<dialog "Tess">> Whatever it is, keep doing it. You're almost pretty. <</dialog>> She tapped the table twice the same friendly punctuation as before and moved to the next customer. Pretty. The word sat in my chest like a dropped coin sinking through deep water. Slow. Heavy. Reaching places that hadn't been touched. Places I didn't know existed. Places that the potion was building or uncovering or both, somewhere underneath the muscle and the stubble and the identity I'd worn for twenty-six years without questioning its fit. Pretty. Not handsome. Not rugged. Not any of the words men got the words I'd been getting my whole adult life, the ones that sat comfortably on a square jaw and broad shoulders and a body that took up space like it owned it. She'd said pretty. A word for different faces. Softer faces. Faces that were changing shape in ways that a barmaid with a gift for reading people could see even when the man wearing the face couldn't. <<dialog "Mira">> What did she say? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Nothing. That I looked rested. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You don't look rested. You look like a man who slept on a bar floor after being carried through a forest with a hole in his leg. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Maybe she has low standards for rested. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> She said something else. I heard her voice change. The pitch shifted the way people's voices shift when they're saying something they didn't plan to say. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> She said I'm almost pretty. <</dialog>> Silence. The kind of silence that has texture thick, loaded, full of things unsaid. <<dialog "Mira">> Pretty. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> It's just a word. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It's a specific word. There are a hundred words for "you look good." Handsome. Striking. Sharp. Fit. She picked pretty. That's not random. That girl reads faces for a living. She chose that word because it's the word her instincts gave her, and her instincts are better than most people's deliberate assessments. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> You're reading too much into it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I'm reading exactly the right amount into it. Which is what I've been doing for the last two days, watching you avoid mirrors and adjust your belt and flinch when your shirt touches your chest. <</dialog>> The booth got very small. The air between us dense. Mira's amber eyes were locked on mine not accusing, not afraid. Determined. The look she wore when she'd been tracking something through the brush and had finally run it to ground and wasn't going to let it bolt. <<dialog "Aldric">> Mira <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> A barmaid who's known you for five days just called you pretty. Your skin is smoother than it was when we arrived. Your jaw has changed shape subtle, but I've been looking at that jaw from across tables and from pillows and from below when you're on top of me, and it's different and you're pretending everything is fine because pretending is easier than whatever the alternative is. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The alternative is <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The alternative is telling me what you already know. What Sera told you. What that potion is doing. Because I can see it, Aldric. Not the way Tess can see it she doesn't have context. I do. I've memorized your body. Every scar, every muscle, every angle and the body I'm looking at right now isn't the body I memorized. <</dialog>> The common room noise washed around us laughter, conversation, the clink of tankards, the creak of furniture. The noise of other people's lives, uncomplicated and unremarkable. Inside the booth, in the six inches of ale-scented air between my face and Mira's, everything was very quiet and very loud at the same time. <<dialog "Aldric">> I don't know what it's doing. Not exactly. Sera said... she said it's changing me. At a foundational level. Not healing changing. The skin, the bones, the everything. She said it's not going to stop. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Changing you into what? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I don't know. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You don't know or you won't say? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I don't know. Sera doesn't know. Nobody knows because the woman who gave me the potion vanished before she could explain what the potion does, and all I have is a body that's doing things without my permission and a barmaid who just called me pretty. <</dialog>> My voice cracked on the last word. Not emotionally physically. The pitch shifted, the tone warping for a half-second into something lighter and less controlled, a hiccup in the vocal machinery that I covered with a cough and Mira covered with a silence that said she'd noticed. She reached across the table. Took my hand. The grip was firm archer's fingers, calloused pads, the hand I'd held in the dark and in the light and in every space between. <<dialog "Mira">> Okay. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Okay? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Okay. I don't need to know what it is yet. I don't need answers you don't have. I just need you to stop pretending that nothing's happening, because the pretending is worse than the happening. I can handle change. I can't handle you lying to me about it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I wasn't lying. I was <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Omitting. Avoiding. Strategically not mentioning. All of which are Aldric Vane synonyms for lying, and I will not have it. Not from you. Not about your body. Not about anything. <</dialog>> She squeezed my hand. Hard enough to hurt, which was her love language. <<dialog "Mira">> We'll figure it out. Ysolde went south. We follow. We find her, we find answers. If the answers are bad, we deal with bad answers the way we deal with everything badly, but together. Agreed? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Agreed. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Good. Now drink your terrible ale and stop looking at your reflection in the tankard. Yes, I can see you doing that. You're not subtle. <</dialog>> I drank my terrible ale. I stopped looking at my reflection in the tankard or tried to, but the curved metal surface kept catching my eye, and every time it did I saw a face that was mine and not mine, the jaw a degree softer than it should have been, the skin a shade smoother, the eyebrow scar the only constant in a landscape of slow-motion change. Across the bar, Tess was wiping another tankard. Circles. Steady. Her eyes sweeping the room, reading faces, filing truths. She caught my gaze and smiled. The quick, freckled smile. Then she moved on. Pretty. The coin was still sinking. > [END THE BARMAID'S EYE] > > Scene 1 (Day -2): Tess established as human lie detector. Reads Aldric's scars, financial status, and emotional state in seconds. Catalogs his baseline face and body. > Scene 2 (Day 0): Tess notices changes she can't name. Says "pretty" the first external, unprompted confirmation from a stranger that something visible is happening. Forces the Mira confrontation where she demands Aldric stop pretending. > > NPC established: Tess recurring Broken Antler presence. Every time Aldric returns to Valdmere, Tess will see him. Her readings become a barometer of the transformation's progress, each observation more specific, more alarming, more undeniable. > > Relationship beat: Mira breaks through Aldric's denial. "I've memorized your body and the body I'm looking at right now isn't the body I memorized." The pretending ends here. What replaces it is rawer and harder and more honest and infinitely more frightening. > > Lenna variant (Branch A only): If Lenna is present in the common room, an optional interaction occurs where she notices the jaw change "Your jaw, too. Something about your jaw." from the context of having been physically intimate with Aldric two days prior. Her observation is more specifically physical because her knowledge of his body is more recent and more tactile.He was sitting against the wall ten feet from freedom, and he couldn't move. The East Gate was Valdmere's lung the great stone archway where the city exhaled travelers, merchants, and soldiers onto the Ashenmoor Road and inhaled them back again. Two guards flanked it, armored, bored, their attention divided between the traffic passing through and the dice game they'd abandoned on the guardhouse table. Neither of them was looking at the boy against the wall. Why would they? He wasn't going anywhere. I noticed him because Mira noticed him first. <<dialog "Mira">> Garrison. <</dialog>> She said it quietly, the single word containing a complete assessment. I followed her gaze. He was nineteen or Twenty. Maybe. The kind of age where youth and adulthood overlap uncomfortably a man's body housing a boy's terror. His face was sharp-boned and hollow-cheeked, the face of someone who hadn't been sleeping well or eating enough or doing either of the things that faces needed to look like they belonged to a functioning human. His eyes were brown and wet and fixed on the cobblestones between his boots with the thousand-yard stare of a man who'd seen something that wouldn't let go of his retinas. Garrison uniform. Regulation cut. But the shoulder insignia the crossed-pike emblem that marked Valdmere's city guard had been ripped off. Not carefully removed, not unpicked. Ripped. The fabric beneath was raw, torn, a wound in the cloth that mirrored something happening underneath it. His pack sat beside him. Stuffed to bursting clothing, a water skin, a rolled blanket strapped to the top with cord that had been tied and retied, the knots speaking of trembling hands. Everything he owned. Everything he could carry. The luggage of someone who was leaving. But he hadn't left. The gate was right there. The road was right there. Three steps and a threshold and whatever waited on the other side freedom or flight or the particular emptiness of a man who's cut himself loose from the only structure he had. Three steps and he'd been sitting there for twenty minutes, according to the guard who'd been ignoring him, and he hadn't taken them. <<dialog "Aldric">> Stay here. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> What are you <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Just give me a minute. <</dialog>> I walked over. My shadow fell across his boots. He flinched the full-body recoil of a soldier expecting punishment, the instinctive cringe of someone whose command structure had taught him that approaching authority meant pain or orders or both. Then his eyes came up. Brown, wet, terrified. They scanned me civilian clothing, sword on hip, no garrison insignia, no rank, no authority. The flinch downgraded from flight-response to rigid wariness. <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm not garrison. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> I know what this looks like. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> It looks like desertion. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> It is desertion. <</dialog>> The honesty was startling. No dissembling, no excuse, no hastily constructed cover story about a leave of absence or a family emergency. Just flat, exhausted admission from a boy who was too scared to lie and too tired to try. <<dialog "Tam">> Desertion is a hanging offense in Valdmere. I know. I don't care. <</dialog>> He said I don't care the way people say it when they care enormously but the thing they care about has been outweighed by something larger and more terrible. Not bravado. Surrender. The white flag of a conscience that couldn't carry what it was being asked to carry. <<dialog "Aldric">> I'm going to sit down. If that's alright. <</dialog>> I didn't wait for permission. I sat. Back against the wall, shoulder to shoulder with a boy who was either a deserter or a whistleblower or just someone whose body had brought him to a threshold his feet refused to cross. <<dialog "Aldric">> Tell me. <</dialog>> [[Ask him why he's deserting|deserter_the_reason]]It came out in fragments. Not a narrative a confession. The kind of story that doesn't flow because the teller keeps stopping to breathe, to swallow, to push past the places where the words have thorns. <<dialog "Tam">> Three months. I've been in the garrison for three months. Standard recruitment signing bonus, room and board, the promise of "honorable service." That's what the recruiter said. Honorable service. It sounded like safety. Like belonging. I was nineteen with no family and no trade and a city that didn't have a place for me, and a man in a uniform told me there was a place, and I believed him. <</dialog>> He pulled at a loose thread on his torn shoulder patch. Wrapped it around his finger. Unwrapped it. <<dialog "Tam">> The first month was fine. Training, drills, patrols. Standard work. I was good at it. Not great I'm not built for great. But reliable. Showed up. Did what I was told. Followed orders. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> What changed? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> The sergeant. Not Harsk Harsk is decent. A different sergeant. Patrol division. Name of Kessler. <</dialog>> He said the name the way Dalla had said Sefton's with the particular flat precision of someone naming a disease they'd survived. <<dialog "Tam">> Kessler started sending recruits on what he called "training exercises." Night patrols along the Ashenmoor Road. Goblin activity surveys. He said it was field experience. Said it would make us better soldiers. Said the garrison needed intelligence on warband movements and the recruits were the best option because we were young, fast, expendable <</dialog>> He caught himself. Swallowed. <<dialog "Tam">> He didn't say expendable. Not out loud. But he meant it. You could hear it in the gaps between his words. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The exercises weren't surveys. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> No. They were combat sweeps. Unsanctioned. Unreported. Kessler was trying to thin the goblin warband before it became a big enough problem to require official garrison deployment which would require official paperwork, which would require admitting that the garrison had let a goblin problem fester for months on his watch. So instead of filing a report and requesting reinforcements like he was supposed to, he sent recruits. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> How many sweeps? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> Four. The first three were they weren't good. Goblins in the dark, tunnels, screaming. But we came back. Bruised, bitten, scared shitless, but alive. We came back and Kessler wrote "training exercise completed" in the log and told us we were becoming real soldiers and sent us to the mess hall for an extra ration. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> The fourth sweep. <</dialog>> Tam's hands stopped moving. The thread hung limp from his finger. His eyes fixed on a point in the middle distance that wasn't a point at all but a memory, vivid and permanent, burned into the backs of his eyelids like a brand. <<dialog "Tam">> Two of us died. <</dialog>> The words came out flat. Quiet. The way facts come out when they're too heavy for emphasis. <<dialog "Tam">> A boy named Edric. Eighteen. He was from a fishing village north of here. He talked about his mother all the time her cooking, her garden, the way she sang when she hung the wash. He'd been in the garrison six weeks. He didn't know how to hold a sword properly. He held it with both hands like a broom because nobody had shown him the grip. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> A woman named Sorcha. Twenty. She was she was good. Better than any of us. Fast, smart, brave in a way that made you brave by proximity. She should have been a sergeant herself. She went into the tunnels first because she always went first and the goblins were waiting and they <</dialog>> He stopped. Breathed. The shallow, controlled breathing of someone holding back something that wanted very badly to come out. <<dialog "Tam">> Their deaths were reported as training accidents. Garrison record says they died during a supervised field exercise. Supervised. Kessler was in his quarters playing cards when it happened. He wasn't within a mile of those tunnels. But the paperwork says supervised, and the families got a condolence payment, and the bodies got a military burial with full honors, and Kessler got a commendation for "proactive threat management" and nobody nobody asked what proactive threat management means when it's two dead recruits in a hole in the ground. <</dialog>> I looked at him. At the torn insignia. At the packed bag. At the hands that had stopped trembling and gone still with the particular rigidity of a body that had spent its last reserves of emotion and was running on structural integrity alone. <<dialog "Tam">> I was there. I was in the rear rank. When the screaming started, I ran. I'm not proud of it. But I'm alive, and they're not, and the man who sent us there is sleeping in an officer's quarter with clean hands and a clean conscience and I can't I can't stand next to him and salute and pretend. I can't do it. I'd rather hang. <</dialog>> The gate was ten feet away. The road was beyond it. The guards were still ignoring us two men against a wall, one in a torn uniform, one with a sword. Not interesting enough to investigate. Not alarming enough to report. <<dialog "Aldric">> What do you want, Tam? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> I want Edric to be alive. I want Sorcha to be alive. I want Kessler to answer for what he did. I want none of this to have happened. I want to go back to the day I signed the recruitment papers and I want to tear them in half and walk away and become a farmer or a baker or anything that doesn't involve standing over a grave and being told it was a training accident. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Since you can't have any of that? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> I want to leave. I want to walk through that gate and keep walking until Valdmere is a memory and Kessler is a name I used to know and none of this can touch me anymore. <</dialog>> He looked at the gate. Ten feet. Three steps. The hardest three steps he'd ever take. <<dialog "Tam">> But I can't. I've been sitting here for I don't know how long and I can't move. My legs won't it's like they're part of the wall. Like the garrison has its hooks in me so deep that even deserting requires permission and nobody's given it. <</dialog>> I sat with him. Let the silence hold for a moment. The gate traffic flowed past merchants, travelers, a woman with a handcart full of apples, two children chasing a dog. Life happening around us, ordinary and oblivious. <<dialog "Aldric">> You don't need permission, Tam. Not from Kessler. Not from the garrison. Not from me. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> Then why can't I move? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Because leaving is the easiest part. Living with having left that's the weight you're feeling. You'll carry it either way. The question is where you want to be carrying it. <</dialog>> He looked at me. The wet brown eyes searching my face for something conviction, maybe. Permission, despite what I'd said. Or just the simple, animal reassurance of another person saying you're not crazy, what happened to you was real, and what you're doing about it makes sense. [[Help him leave|deserter_help_leave]] [[Talk him into staying|deserter_talk_stay]] [[Walk past|deserter_walk_past]]<<dialog "Aldric">> Stand up. <</dialog>> He looked at me. The brown eyes wide, questioning. <<dialog "Aldric">> Stand up. We're going through the gate. <</dialog>> I pulled my traveling cloak from my pack the heavy wool one, road-stained and nondescript, the kind of garment that made a person look like every other traveler on every other road. I held it out to him. <<dialog "Aldric">> Put this on. Covers the uniform. You're not a garrison soldier walking through the East Gate. You're a civilian traveling with two sellswords. Nobody looks twice at that. <</dialog>> Tam stared at the cloak. At me. At the gate. <<dialog "Tam">> You'd why? You don't know me. You don't owe me <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I know two people are dead because a man with authority used it to cover his own failures, and I know you're alive and trying to live with that, and I know the gate is ten feet away and your legs won't take you there alone. That's enough. <</dialog>> Mira appeared beside me. She'd been listening of course she had, half-elf ears and the strategic patience of a woman who gathered intelligence the way other people gathered firewood. She looked at Tam. Looked at the cloak. Looked at me. <<dialog "Mira">> We're doing this? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> We're doing this. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Fine. But we walk at a normal pace. No hurrying. No looking over shoulders. We're travelers, we're bored, we're heading east because there's work on the road. That's the story if anyone asks, which they won't, because nobody cares about three people walking through a gate. <</dialog>> She was right. Nobody would care. The gate guards processed hundreds of travelers daily, and their threat assessment was calibrated for incoming danger, not outgoing deserters. A torn insignia under a borrowed cloak wouldn't register in their peripheral vision. Tam stood. His legs wobbled the particular instability of a body that had been frozen in one position for too long and had forgotten that motion was an option. He took the cloak. Pulled it over his shoulders. The heavy wool swallowed the garrison uniform, the torn patch, the identity of a soldier who'd decided to stop being one. He fastened the clasp. His hands were shaking. But they were moving. <<dialog "Aldric">> Ready? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> No. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Good enough. <</dialog>> We walked. Three abreast Aldric on the left, Mira on the right, Tam in the middle, the borrowed cloak hiding everything except his face and his fear. The gate guards didn't look up. The dice game on the guardhouse table was apparently more interesting than three travelers heading east, which was probably for the best because Tam's face was the color of old parchment and his eyes were doing something complicated that involved tears and willpower in roughly equal measure. We passed through the arch. The stone ceiling above us, three feet thick, the accumulated weight of Valdmere's defensive history pressing down. Then air. Light. The road opening ahead packed earth, muddy from rain, stretching east toward the Ashenmoor forest and the rolling farmland beyond it. Tam stopped. Stood in the road. Breathed. The air didn't taste different outside the walls. It was the same air salt from the river, earth from the fields, the faint vegetal rot of late autumn. But Tam breathed it like a man surfacing from underwater, gulping it in with the desperate relief of someone whose lungs had been compressed for months and were finally, finally expanding. <<dialog "Tam">> Thank you. <</dialog>> His voice was thin. A wire vibrating at its breaking point. <<dialog "Tam">> I don't I don't know where to go. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> North. Farming villages along the river. They always need hands, especially before winter. You're young, you're strong, you can hold a hoe as well as a sword. Better, probably hoes don't stab back. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> Will they ask about the uniform? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Not if you burn it first. Find a stream, wash it off, start clean. Nobody in a farming village cares where you came from. They care whether you can lift a bale and wake up at dawn. <</dialog>> Tam nodded. Adjusted the pack on his shoulders. The straps dug into the cloak too heavy, poorly balanced, the luggage of someone who'd packed in panic rather than planning. He'd learn to pack lighter. He'd learn a lot of things, out on the road, in the villages, in the long slow process of becoming someone who didn't carry a dead friend's name like a stone in his chest. He started walking. North, as Mira suggested. The road curved toward the river, and he followed it, his boots leaving prints in the mud that the next rain would erase. After ten paces, he stopped. Turned. <<dialog "Tam">> The sergeant. His name is Kessler. If anyone ever if there's ever a way to <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> We'll remember the name. <</dialog>> Kessler. I filed it where I filed all the names of people who used authority as a weapon against the people under their protection. Next to Sefton. Next to Grunn. A growing list that said something about the kind of world we lived in and the kind of people who ran it. <<dialog "Tam">> He has records. In his office at the garrison. Patrol logs. The real ones, not the ones he files with command. He keeps duplicates dates, routes, casualties. Everything he covered up. He keeps them because he's the kind of man who documents his own crimes. In case he ever needs to prove he was in control. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Why are you telling me this? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> Because I can't go back. But someone should. Someone should walk into that office and take those records and make them mean something. Edric's mother thinks her son died in a training exercise. Sorcha's family thinks the same. They deserve the truth. Even if the truth doesn't bring anyone back, they deserve it. <</dialog>> He held my gaze for a long moment. Nineteen years old. Brown eyes. The face of a boy who was learning, right now, in this moment, that courage wasn't the absence of fear but the decision to act while you were drowning in it. <<dialog "Tam">> Thank you. For opening the door. <</dialog>> He turned. Walked. Grew smaller. A figure in a borrowed cloak on a muddy road, heading north toward farming villages and silence and the long, complicated work of building a life that didn't have a dead man's name attached to it. I watched him until he disappeared around the bend. <<dialog "Mira">> Kessler. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Kessler. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Another name. Another thread. You collect them the way other people collect debts. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Maybe that's exactly what they are. <</dialog>> She looked at me. The amber eyes doing their calculation the one that weighed what I'd just done against what it had cost us (a cloak, ten minutes, nothing material) and what it had gained (a name, a location, a thread that connected to the garrison's institutional rot like a root connecting to the trunk of a poisoned tree). <<dialog "Mira">> You gave him your cloak. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I have another one. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You don't. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I'll buy one. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> With what money? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> With the money I'll earn from the work we'll find. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> That's aspirational budgeting, which is your specialty and also the reason we're broke. But <</dialog>> She paused. The arrowhead came out. Click against her canine. The thinking sound. <<dialog "Mira">> But you did a good thing. A stupid thing. An expensive thing. A thing that won't change anything about Kessler or the garrison or the two dead recruits rotting in a military cemetery under a headstone that says "training accident." But a good thing. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Thank you. I think. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You're welcome. I think. <</dialog>> We stood outside the East Gate and looked at the road and didn't walk down it. Not yet. Not today. [[Chat with Mira|deserter_resolution]]I sat down next to him. Back against the wall. Two men at a threshold. <<dialog "Aldric">> I was nineteen once. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> Yeah? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Nineteen and scared and standing at a crossroads where every direction looked like a mistake. My father had just died. Drank himself into the ground after the local lord seized our farm. My mother moved in with relatives. My brother apprenticed to a smith and I was standing in a field that didn't belong to us anymore, holding a sword I barely knew how to use, staring at a world that didn't seem to have a place for me in it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> What did you do? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I left. Took the sword, took the road, became a sellsword because it was the only trade that didn't require land or a guild membership or a conscience. Spent seven years fighting other people's wars, sleeping in other people's cities, carrying other people's problems for money and I've never stopped leaving. Every city is temporary. Every contract is a countdown. I walk in, I do the work, I walk out. That's the whole story. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> That's what you're telling me to do? Leave? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> No. I'm telling you what leaving costs. Because you're looking at that gate like it's salvation, and it might be. But it's also a door that only opens one direction. Once you're through it, you're a deserter. You can never come back. You can never stand in front of Kessler and say his name to someone who can do something about it. You can never look Edric's mother in the eye and tell her what really happened. <</dialog>> Tam's hands tightened on the torn insignia patch. The thread he'd been pulling wound around his finger like a tourniquet. <<dialog "Aldric">> Running is easy. I know I've been doing it for seven years. The hard thing is staying. Not because staying is safe. Not because staying is right. But because the people who died in those tunnels deserve a witness, and a witness who runs can't testify. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> If I stay and Kessler sends me into another tunnel? <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Then you refuse and he writes you up for insubordination and you tell whoever handles the write-up why you refused and you name the dead. Edric. Sorcha. Out loud. On the record. Where someone who isn't Kessler has to hear it. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Tam">> That's they'll make my life <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Hell? Probably. [[Check the East Gate|east_garrison]]The East Garrison squatted at the junction of the Market District and the east road like a bulldog that had been told to sit and had interpreted the command as a personal philosophy. It wasn't elegant. Valdmere's garrison had never been elegant it had been effective, which in military architecture meant thick walls, small windows, and the general aesthetic charm of a clenched fist. The stone was stained with decades of weather and what might have been the residue of thrown vegetables from citizens who considered the garrison a necessary evil and expressed their feelings about the "evil" part through the medium of overripe produce. The mercenary board was mounted on the outer wall, exposed to the elements, which meant exposed to rain, sun, pigeon droppings, and the slow degradation of hope that came from watching the same postings fade to illegibility while nothing better replaced them. [[Check the Sparring Yard|board_sergeant_yard]]The sparring yard was a packed-dirt rectangle behind the garrison, marked with chalk lines that had been redrawn so many times the ground was more chalk than dirt. A weapons rack stood against the far wall practice blades in various sizes, wooden shields, padded quarterstaves. Everything was worn, dented, well-used the equipment of an institution that had been training soldiers longer than most of the soldiers had been alive. A young garrison soldier was waiting in the center of the yard. Twenty, maybe. Eager. It was heavier than my real blade weighted for training, the edge blunted to a rounded safety margin that would leave bruises instead of wounds. The young soldier stood in the yard. Ready. His eyes bright with the particular intensity of someone about to prove something to himself. I stepped into the ring. <<dialog "Soldier">> Ready when you are. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Go ahead. <</dialog>> He opened with a high diagonal. The blade came down exactly as Mira predicted right-to-left, textbook angle, the manual's opening strike delivered with the full-body commitment of a soldier who'd practiced it a thousand times and believed in it the way some people believed in prayer. It was clean. Well-executed. The kind of strike that would end a fight against an opponent who'd never seen it before. I'd seen it before. About six thousand times. From training partners, from bandits, from goblins who didn't use swords but swung their cleavers on the same angle because diagonal-down was what bodies naturally did when they wanted to hit something. I parried. A smooth, compact deflection blade meeting blade at the optimal intercept point, redirecting the diagonal's force rather than stopping it. The impact vibrated through my arms, the practice sword's extra weight making the parry harder than it would have been with my own blade. But the technique was sound and the angle was right and the soldier's strike slid off mine like water off stone. I stepped left. His blade carried past me, the overcommitment that Mira had predicted pulling his weight forward and his guard open. His center line was exposed the vertical axis of the body, sternum to navel, where every critical target lived. I could have taken it. A thrust, a cut, a pommel strike any of a dozen options that would have ended the spar in the first exchange. But Mira had said economy, not brutality. And Harsk was watching from the garrison gate, his mug of tea/poison in one hand, his squint narrowed to maximum evaluation intensity. I checked the soldier's shoulder with my pommel a short, controlled tap, firm enough to throw his balance without injuring. He stumbled backward, his feet scrambling for purchase on the chalked dirt, his guard collapsing from textbook to improvised in a single heartbeat. He recovered. To his credit he recovered. Reset his stance, raised his blade, came at me again. This time faster, more aggressive, the particular fury of a young fighter who'd been embarrassed by the first exchange and was determined not to repeat it. He feinted left. Good a feint meant he was thinking, not just swinging. He followed with a low cut aimed at my leading knee also good, a dirty shot that most training partners wouldn't expect because training was supposed to be civilized. I wasn't civilized. I'd learned to fight from other mercenaries in real combats against real threats, and my training hadn't included any of the gentlemanly conventions that garrison academies liked to pretend existed in actual combat. I checked the low cut with a downward parry, rotated my blade under his, and lifted. His sword went up. His arms went with it. His guard opened completely. I placed the flat of my practice blade against his throat. Gently. A touch. The universal signal in every sparring tradition: I had you. The yard was quiet. Someone who knows the ground. Someone who can ask questions without attracting the kind of attention that makes questions dangerous. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> I might know someone. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> You always might know someone. It's your other compulsion. <</dialog>> [[Check in with Undercity contact|board_daughter_contact]]<<dialog "Aldric">> The goblin survey. Ten silver. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> The one that involves going back to the area where goblins live. In tunnels. Underground. Where my bow is useless and your judgment is historically questionable. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Survey. Not combat. We count them from a distance. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> Counting goblins from a distance is like watching fire from a distance. It's perfectly safe until the wind changes. And the wind always changes. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Aldric">> Ten silver, Mira. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> I heard you the first time. My objections are on record. Let's go count goblins. <</dialog>> She said "let's go count goblins" the way most people said "let's go to the dentist" with the resigned certainty of someone who knew the experience would be unpleasant and was choosing to endure it because the alternative was worse. [[Choose Goblin Survey|board_sergeant_resolution]]We walked out of the garrison. Through the gate. Past the guards who glanced at us with the professional disinterest of men whose job was to look at people and whose survival depended on not finding most of them interesting. I had the chit in my pocket. The registration. The piece of paper that said Aldric Vane sellsword registered and that opened doors that had been sealed to us three hours ago. And somewhere inside the garrison, on Harsk's desk, in a ledger that was probably as old as the building itself, a line of ink sat drying on a page. Male. 6'1". 190 lbs. Broad shoulders. Green eyes. Scar through left eyebrow. A description. A snapshot. A record of a body at a specific moment in a specific place, captured in the permanent medium of ink on paper by a man who didn't care about the body and only cared about the accuracy. Every word precise. Every measurement correct. <<dialog "Mira">> What? <</dialog>> She'd caught me looking back at the garrison gate. The stone arch. The walls. The building where a ledger held my name and my body's exact description and would hold them indefinitely, because garrison ledgers didn't expire and ink didn't fade and Harsk's handwriting was as permanent as the stone it was housed in. <<dialog "Aldric">> Nothing. Just thinking. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> About? <</dialog>> About records. About the particular weight of being described measured, documented, pinned to a page with the clinical precision of a man who turned bodies into data. About the fact that somewhere in that building, a version of me existed that would outlast whatever version of me walked out of this city. A fixed point. An anchor. I didn't say any of this. <<dialog "Aldric">> About whether eight silver is worth a night in a warehouse. <</dialog>> <<dialog "Mira">> It is. Let's eat. <</dialog>> We walked. The garrison receded behind us. The Market District opened ahead noise, smells, the churn of commerce and humanity doing what it always did, regardless of what was recorded in what ledger by what sergeant in what stone-walled fortress at the edge of a city that didn't care about any of us. The chit sat in my pocket. Light as paper. Heavy as a name carved into stone. > [END THE BOARD AND THE SERGEANT] > > Item acquired: Garrison registration chit (unlocks sealed postings on the mercenary board) > Record created: Physical description of Aldric in the garrison ledger Male, 6'1", 190 lbs, broad shoulders, green eyes, scar through left eyebrow, scar on right ribcage. This record becomes a ticking time bomb when Aldric returns mid-transformation the body that walks up to Harsk's desk will match exactly one detail (the eyebrow scar) and nothing else. > NPC established: Harsk garrison sergeant, professional, scarred, laconic. Respects results, not promises. "Your best is statistically insufficient." Returns mid-game as a gatekeeper who has to reconcile the woman in front of him with the man in his ledger. > Sealed postings: Three optional mini-quests available (warehouse security, missing daughter, goblin survey). Each can be pursued or saved for later. > Sparring soldier: Unnamed but friendly.
